name: A Culture Orbital
blurb: A ring three million kilometres across, spun for gravity, with engineered weather and no laws, money, work or death. Ask the Mind politely and it will build you a continent.

name: A Wraith Hive Ship
blurb: A grown ship the size of a city, with corridors that flex, dormitories of cocooned people being kept alive for later, and a queen who will ask you a question you are not able to lie to.
about: The Wraith hibernate for centuries and wake to cull, and the hive is the best thing Atlantis ever designed: nothing is built, everything is grown, and the humans stored in the walls are livestock. The genuinely frightening idea underneath the show is that the Ancients fought these and lost, and left the galaxy to them.

name: Aboard the Nautilus
blurb: A submarine with a pipe organ, a library of twelve thousand volumes and a captain who has renounced the surface entirely. Meals are exclusively from the sea.

name: Abydos
blurb: The first world through the Stargate: a desert of pyramids and naquadah mines, whose people were taken from Egypt thousands of years ago and taught to worship the being who took them.

name: Aerilon
blurb: Cold fields, hard work and the accent Gaius Baltar spent an entire career pretending he did not have. Aerilon feeds the Colonies and is looked down on by every single one of them.
about: The show's class politics live here. Aerilon is poor, agricultural and mocked, and its most famous son changed his voice to get out — so when Baltar's real accent slips in the final season it is the most revealing thing he ever does. The eleven colonies that eat Aerilon's food never once vote in its interest.

name: Ahch-To
blurb: A green island of stone huts and impossible steps in a cold ocean, the first Jedi temple, and thousands of very confident seabirds.

name: Airstrip One
blurb: London as a province of Oceania: rationed, bombed, watched from every wall, and at war with a power whose identity has always been the one it is at war with now.
about: Orwell wrote it on Jura while dying of tuberculosis, and set it in a Britain of post-war shortages he had actually lived through — the gin is bad, the razor blades have run out, the lift doesn't work. The Ministry of Truth rewrites yesterday's papers daily; Newspeak is designed so that certain thoughts become unsayable and therefore unthinkable. Almost every English word for surveillance now comes from this book.

name: Alderaan
blurb: Snow-capped mountains above grasslands and glass-spired cities, a world with no weapons and a two-thousand-year peace. Visit while you can.
about: Alderaan exists in the films for about ninety seconds and only in order to be destroyed, which is the point: it is the Death Star's argument, made once. Everything else known about it — the pacifism, the art, the royal house that adopted Leia — was filled in afterwards by people trying to make the loss land harder. It works.

name: Almaren
blurb: An island in a lake in the middle of a world lit by two enormous lamps, in the age before there were seasons, deaths or history. It lasted until somebody knocked the lamps over.
about: The Valar's first home, in the Spring of Arda: constant light, everything growing at once, no night anywhere. Melkor threw down the Lamps of Illuin and Ormal, the shape of the world broke, the seas came in and the Spring ended — and the Valar left for Aman and shut the door. Everything afterwards in Tolkien is people trying to rebuild something ruined before the story starts.

name: Alqualondë
blurb: The Swanhaven: a harbour of pearl and lamplit arches, swan-prowed ships, and the finest mariners in the world. The quays remember the one night the Noldor came down and took the ships by force.
about: The Teleri built Alqualondë out of pearl the Noldor gave them, and it is where the Kinslaying happened — elves killing elves on the quays over boats. That is the crime the Doom of Mandos hangs on, and the reason the war in Beleriand goes the way it does. The Teleri afterwards would not lend a ship to anybody for an age, and they were entitled.

name: Andoria
blurb: An ice moon whose cities are carved deep below the surface, home to a proud, quick-tempered, four-parent species who founded the Federation and remain slightly annoyed about the paperwork.

name: Androzani Minor
blurb: A hollow, unstable moon of mud bursts and gun-runners, where raw spectrox — the most valuable substance in existence, and lethal before refining — is scraped out of the caves.

name: Andúnië
blurb: The sunset coast: a bay of fragrant evergreens brought from the West, elven ships arriving with gifts, and the last households in Númenor still on speaking terms with the elves once that stopped being wise.
about: The Lords of Andúnië led the Faithful, and Tolkien plainly loved the place — Eldalondë the Green, where the trees out of Tol Eressëa grew and the whole bay smelled of them. When the kings turned, the Faithful were moved to the far side of the island for being suspicious, and the line of Andúnië became the line of Elendil, which is to say the line of Aragorn.

name: Angband
blurb: Three slag-mountains over a pit that goes down for miles, garrisoned by everything Morgoth ever made. The original dark tower, of which every later one is a copy, and comfortably the worst address in any age.
about: Everything in the First Age comes out of this hole: the balrogs, the first dragons, the orc-hosts, the Silmarils nailed into an iron crown. Fingolfin rode to the gate alone, challenged Morgoth to single combat, wounded him seven times and died doing it — the only occasion anyone hurt him. Shutting the place took the host of the Valar and the drowning of a subcontinent.

name: Angmar
blurb: The Witch-king's own realm, six centuries of it, now a scatter of frozen ruins at Carn Dûm where nothing grows and the wind does all the talking.
about: Angmar existed to destroy Arnor, and did, kingdom by kingdom, over six hundred years. It was broken at Fornost in 1975 by Gondor's fleet and the elves of Lindon, and its sorcerer-king rode away laughing — to Minas Ithil, and the head of the Nazgûl. The barrow-wights he sent south into the Downs are still there, which tells you how thoroughly the place was cleaned up.

name: Ankh-Morpork
blurb: The Discworld's great, filthy, thriving city, built on the silt of a river too thick to drink and too thin to plough. Run by a tyrant who is very good at it, and by guilds for everything including thieves.
about: A million people, several dozen species and one Patrician. The Guild of Thieves is licensed and issues receipts; the Watch has grown from three drunks to a functioning police force; the Post Office works again. Pratchett used it to write about every civic institution in turn — the mint, the newspaper, the railway, the opera house — which is why the city changes measurably from book to book. Nothing in it is safe and everything in it is funny.

name: Apalapucia
blurb: Voted the second most beautiful planet in the galaxy — glorious silver colonnades, two suns, and a quarantine facility where a lifetime passes in a day so the dying can be visited without catching it.

name: Argelius II
blurb: A hedonistic port world with a total prohibition on violence, famous for its cafés, dancers and complete lack of crime — a reputation that took a knock during a memorable series of murders.

name: Ariel
blurb: A Core world of white towers and hovercars with the best hospitals in the Verse — all of it beautiful, none of it yours. Excellent medicine, provided you can produce identification.
about: Ariel is the crew's one proper look at Core living, and they go there to rob a hospital. It is also where Simon finally gets his sister scanned and learns what was done to her brain: the plot of the whole show turns on a diagnosis obtained by fraud, in a building that would never have let any of them in the front door.

name: Armenelos
blurb: The City of the Kings: gardens on every terrace, a fountain court, a silver crown and a white tree in the middle that everybody is extremely careful about. Peak Númenor, shortly before the fall.
about: Armenelos was the richest city any mortal built, and by the end it had a temple to Morgoth in it with black smoke going up. Ar-Pharazôn's fleet sailed from here to make war on the Valar and the island went under nine days later. What survives is nine ships, four heirlooms, a seedling of the white tree, and a family that becomes the kings of Gondor.

name: Arrakis
blurb: The only source of the spice, and the harshest inhabited world known. Water is currency, worms are three hundred metres long, and the Fremen do not need your help.

name: Asgard
blurb: A golden city on a floating disc at the end of a rainbow bridge, full of immortals who consider a thousand years a reasonable length of time to hold a grudge.
about: Norse myth reworked by Kirby into something closer to space opera — the Aesir are aliens, the Bifrost is a transit system, and Odin's throne room is drawn like a cathedral built by someone who has never heard of restraint. Heimdall stands at the bridge and sees everything in all nine realms, which makes him both the setting's best character and its biggest plot problem. Ragnarök is not avoidable; it is scheduled.

name: Asshai by the Shadow
blurb: A city built entirely of greasy black stone that drinks the light, at the end of the world, where nothing grows, nothing breeds, and everyone wears a mask.
about: Almost nothing is confirmed about Asshai, which is exactly why it works — Martin gives you a handful of details (the black stone, the sunless harbour, the shadowbinders) and lets the gap do the rest. It has no children. Its food is all imported. The river runs black and the fish caught in it are blind and deformed. Melisandre came from here.

name: Atlantis
blurb: Concentric rings of land and water, walls sheathed in orichalcum, and an empire that grew arrogant and was swallowed in a single day and night.

name: Atlantis, Lantea
blurb: The Ancients' city-ship, floating on an empty ocean in another galaxy — spires of glass and alloy, ten thousand years abandoned, and a very long way from anyone who could come and help.

name: Azkaban
blurb: A fortress on a rock in the North Sea guarded by things that feed on happiness. Nobody had escaped in three hundred years, and then two people did in four.
about: Dementors are the best thing Rowling invented, because she wrote them out of her own depression rather than out of folklore: they take the good and leave you with the worst of what you have. The counter-charm requires a genuinely happy memory, which is the point — and it is taught to a thirteen-year-old by the only adult who understands the problem.

name: Ba'ku
blurb: Six hundred people farming a valley inside a nebula, where metaphasic radiation from the rings stops anyone ageing. They gave up warp drive on purpose and seem entirely happy about it.

name: Babylon 4
blurb: A station that vanished four hours after going online — twice: once forwards, and once a thousand years back, to be handed over as a war base to people who died long before you were born.
about: Babylon 4's disappearance is set up in the first season and paid off in the third, when the crew steal it themselves and tow it into the past. Sinclair goes with it, becomes Valen, and wins a war that has been in the history books for a millennium. Closed time loops rarely get tidier, and nobody involved gets to keep the memory.

name: Babylon 5
blurb: Five miles of rotating steel in neutral space, built so five species could argue instead of shoot. A quarter of a million residents, a garden in the middle, and a downbelow you should avoid.

name: Backwards Earth
blurb: An Earth where time runs the other way: meals are un-eaten, haircuts grow back in, and a bar brawl starts with everyone bleeding and ends with the furniture repaired and everybody friends.
about: The best idea the show ever had and the cheapest to film — run the tape backwards and have the cast learn their lines phonetically. The crew stage a reverse pub fight as a public service, beginning with a wrecked bar and finishing with an orderly room, and it still works because the logic is followed all the way through.

name: Bajor
blurb: A deeply devout agrarian world rebuilding after fifty years of occupation, with terraced farms, monasteries full of Orbs, and a wormhole overhead the Bajorans call the Celestial Temple.

name: Battlestar Galactica
blurb: A forty-year-old warship halfway through being turned into a museum, which is exactly why she is still flying: no networked computers, no wireless, nothing for a Cylon to walk into.
about: The premise turns on obsolescence — Galactica survives the fall because Adama refused to network her systems, and everything modern died in minutes. She then spends four years as the only home fifty thousand people have: a flight deck, a memorial wall of photographs nobody takes down, and a commander who talks to her hull as it starts to fail.

name: Beaumonde
blurb: An industrial world of refinery haze and dockside bars, where a straightforward job goes wrong in a place called the Maidenhead and a girl who has been quiet all year takes down an entire room.
about: Beaumonde is where the Verse actually works: refineries, docks, and the kind of bar nobody looks up in. It is also where River is triggered by a subliminal advertisement, which is the moment Serenity stops being a heist film and becomes a story about exactly what the Alliance did to a fourteen-year-old.

name: Beauxbatons
blurb: A palace of fountains and ice sculpture in the mountains of southern France, where the food is superb, the uniforms are silk, and everyone is unbearably polite about the draughts in your castle.
about: Rowling gives Beauxbatons about six pages and every one of them is about class: a school that arrives in a flying carriage drawn by winged horses, asks whether the bouillabaisse is available, and finds Hogwarts cold. Madame Maxime is also the only head teacher in the series better dressed than the Minister for Magic.

name: Beorn's House
blurb: A wooden hall in a clover meadow with bees the size of your thumb, honey-cakes, cream, and a host who is a very large man in the evening and something else after dark. House rule: stay indoors.
about: Beorn is a skin-changer, a vegetarian, keeps animals that wait at table, and hates goblins with a completeness that settles the Battle of Five Armies when he turns up in bear-shape at the end of it. His descendants the Beornings hold the High Pass and the Old Ford afterwards and charge a stiff toll for both. Best meal in The Hobbit, and there is real competition.

name: Betazed
blurb: A warm, gracious world of gardens, lakes and telepaths, where weddings are conducted entirely naked and nobody thinks that is odd. Privacy is a concept you will need to renegotiate.

name: Better Than Life
blurb: A total-immersion game that reads your desires and grants all of them: the mansion, the marriage, the money, the applause. Players starve to death in the chair with a smile on. Guilt is the only exit.
about: The sharpest thing Grant Naylor wrote — a paradise powered by your own subconscious, so a man who hates himself will sabotage it from the inside without ever understanding why. Rimmer's fantasy collapses into a tax demand and a wife who leaves him, because at some level that is what he believes he has coming.

name: Beyond the Wall
blurb: Free Folk, giants, mammoths and something much worse coming south. Genuinely unspoilt. Genuinely will kill you.

name: Biosyn Valley
blurb: A private alpine sanctuary in northern Italy where a biotech company keeps the world's loose dinosaurs, studies amber, and has a very good staff canteen above an underground research campus.
about: Dominion's best idea is the least dinosaur-shaped one: a corporation that gathers the animals for genuinely stated conservation reasons and is also quietly engineering locusts to eat everybody else's crops. The valley itself is the franchise's prettiest setting — limestone walls, pine, snow above the treeline, and something enormous in the trees.

name: Boreth
blurb: A cold monastery world where Klingon clerics wait for Kahless to return, guard a set of time crystals, and will let you look into any future you like on the strict condition you then live it.

name: Bowie Base One, Mars
blurb: The first human colony on Mars, a tidy dome of hydroponics and glaciers, on the specific day in 2059 that history records everyone dying. The view is exceptional.

name: Braavos
blurb: A city of canals in a lagoon, founded by escaped slaves, run by banks, and guarded by a colossus. Superb food, water-dancing, and a temple you should not visit twice.

name: Bree
blurb: A crossroads town where Men and Hobbits drink in the same room and everyone notices strangers. The Prancing Pony does a good pint and a poor job of keeping secrets.

name: Brobdingnag
blurb: A land of giants where the wasps are the size of partridges and a fall from a table is fatal. The king considers our species a pernicious little race of vermin, and he has a point.

name: Buckland & the Old Forest
blurb: The Shire's odd corner, where hobbits keep boats and lock their doors, backing onto a wood whose trees move the paths at night and do not like people.
about: The Old Forest is the first genuinely frightening thing in The Lord of the Rings, and it happens twenty miles from home. Old Man Willow swallows two hobbits; Tom Bombadil, who Tolkien never explained and refused to, sings them out again. Peter Jackson cut all of it, which is defensible and still a shame.

name: Cair Paravel
blurb: The seat of Narnia's kings and queens, on a headland above the eastern sea, with four thrones that stay empty until the right four people arrive.
about: The castle stands where the Great River meets the ocean, and by the later books it is a ruin on an island, because Narnian time runs at a speed nobody in England can predict. Its throne room is the point of the whole country: Narnia is repeatedly saved by children who are told, and eventually believe, that they were always meant to be royalty. Feasts here are described at length and are the best argument for going.

name: Caladan
blurb: A green ocean world of rain, cliffs and fishing fleets — the Atreides homeworld, and everything Arrakis is not. Leaving it was the mistake.

name: Camelot
blurb: One brief shining moment of a castle, a round table with no head, and a kingdom that runs on oaths. It ends badly. Everyone knows it ends badly.

name: Candlekeep
blurb: A fortress library on a crag above the sea, holding every book worth keeping. The entry fee is one book they do not already have, and they usually already have it.
about: The monks of the Binder keep the largest collection in Faerûn, and the admission price — a written work of genuine value — is the most elegant gate in fantasy. You get a month inside. Nobody may remove a book, copy is permitted, and the wards are unpleasant about theft. Baldur's Gate opens here, which means an entire generation's first D&D memory is a library.

name: Canton, Higgins' Moon
blurb: A company town on a moon that produces exactly one thing — mud — worked by indentured labour who have made a folk hero of a mercenary who dropped stolen money on them by accident. There is a statue.
about: Jaynestown is the funniest episode of Firefly and the meanest: the Mudders sing about a man who never intended to help anyone, and when they find out the truth they keep the song anyway. Higgins' Moon is what the Verse does to a workforce with no ship of its own — everything is owed to the company, and the mud is not optional.

name: Caprica
blurb: The wealthiest of the Twelve Colonies — beaches, universities, glass towers and a pyramid league — photographed here on a good day, shortly before it stopped being habitable.

name: Cardassia Prime
blurb: A hot, dry world of brutalist architecture and enthusiastic surveillance, where trials conclude before they begin and the literature is genuinely magnificent. Dress warmly; they keep it at 30°C.

name: Casterly Rock
blurb: A castle carved into a mountain above a gold mine that has never run dry. Three times the height of the Wall, and every inch of it paid for.

name: Centauri Prime
blurb: A faded empire that still throws the best parties in the galaxy — opera, palace intrigue, exceptional drink, and a court where every compliment is a manoeuvre and the hair indicates rank.

name: Century Work Camp
blurb: A holding and disposal facility where prisoners are barcoded across the forearm and put to work clearing bodies. Kyle Reese grew up in one of these. He does not talk about it much.
about: The camps are the reason Reese is the way he is — a man who has never seen a working light bulb, never had a childhood, and reacts to 1984 Los Angeles as though it were a foreign country, which it is. Skynet keeps humans alive to shift rubble, and the barcode on the arm is the film's cheapest and most effective piece of horror.

name: Ceti Alpha V
blurb: Once habitable, until the neighbouring planet exploded and shifted its orbit. Now a sandstorm-scoured shell with one surviving lifeform, a burrowing eel, and some extremely aggrieved marooned colonists.

name: Charn
blurb: A vast dead city under a swollen red sun, where a queen spoke one word and every living thing but herself stopped. There is a bell in the hall, and a sign inviting you to ring it.
about: Lewis's coldest invention: an entire world killed by a single act of spite, preserved as an empty museum of its own greatness. The temptation of the bell — a hand-lettered verse daring the reader to strike it — is one of children's literature's best traps, because you already know the child will, and so would you. Jadis leaves Charn and becomes the White Witch of Narnia.

name: Chulak
blurb: Forested world of the Jaffa, warrior-servants who carry a larval god in their belly in exchange for perfect health. A stern, honourable, tattooed culture, currently reconsidering the arrangement.

name: Cimmeria
blurb: A grey land of cloud, crag and gloom that produces nothing but iron-hard people and a marked disinclination to stay in it. Conan left as soon as he could.
about: Howard wrote a poem about Cimmeria before he wrote a story set there, and the poem is better: 'a gloomy land that seems to hold all winds and clouds and dreams'. The Cimmerians are barbarians in the technical sense — no cities, no writing, no kings — and Howard's whole argument is that this makes them more honest than the civilisations they raid. The gods here are not worth praying to and everybody knows it.

name: Cimmeria
blurb: A Norse-looking world of longhouses and standing stones, protected by a device that strips a Goa'uld out of its host and drops it in a labyrinth. The locals call it Thor's Hammer.
about: Cimmeria is where Stargate's mythology clicks into place: the Asgard are the Norse gods, they protect human worlds from the Goa'uld, and the protection is a machine. Teal'c gets caught by it, and the team have to destroy the one thing keeping the whole planet safe in order to get him out — which comes back on them three seasons later.

name: Cirith Ungol
blurb: A stair, a tunnel and a tower, in that order. The tunnel is occupied. Nobody has ever recommended this route and two hobbits took it anyway.
about: Shelob is older than Sauron's service and keeps the pass for reasons of her own. The tower above was built by Gondor to keep things in, and now holds a garrison that wipes itself out in a quarrel over a mithril shirt — the one piece of luck in the whole journey. It is the most claustrophobic thing Tolkien wrote and the only way into Mordor on foot.

name: Cittàgazze
blurb: A warm Mediterranean city of cafés and shuttered palazzi, entirely empty of adults. The Spectres ate them. The children are fine, until they aren't.
about: The city of magpies sits at a crossroads between worlds, which is why so many windows open onto it. Its people made the subtle knife, cut too many holes, and let the Spectres in — creatures that consume adult consciousness and leave the body standing. Children can't see them and are ignored by them, so Cittàgazze is a beautiful abandoned resort run by feral teenagers. Pullman's most effective horror image, achieved with no gore at all.

name: Clavius Base & TMA-1
blurb: An American moon base running a cover story about an epidemic, and a forty-metre excavation at Tycho containing a black slab that was buried deliberately four million years ago and is now screaming at Jupiter.
about: The middle section is a procedural: a committee, a briefing room, sandwiches on a moonbus, and a group of professionals walking down a ramp to photograph the object. Then the sun hits it and it transmits, and everybody on screen puts their hands to their helmets. Kubrick lets the noise run far longer than is comfortable.

name: Cloud City, Bespin
blurb: A tibanna-gas mining platform floating in the habitable band of a gas giant. Superb sunsets, excellent dining, and the hospitality has a poor historical record.

name: Coruscant
blurb: A single city covering an entire planet, a thousand levels deep. The upper levels have opera and senators; the lower levels have everything else.

name: Crystal Peak
blurb: A Cold War command bunker inside a granite mountain, stocked for a war that already happened, with blast doors that take a while to close. Not the place you were promised. The only one still standing.
about: Terminator 3 does the one thing the series had refused to do: it lets Judgment Day happen. Connor arrives at Crystal Peak expecting the system core and finds an obsolete fallout shelter — the mission was always to survive it, not prevent it. The last shot is a radio room filling with distress calls and one man realising the job just started.

name: Cuiviénen
blurb: A starlit bay in the far east where the first elves woke up and spent an age naming things and singing. No sun, no moon, no history yet. The quietest place in the legendarium.
about: The elves woke here under the stars before the sun existed, which is why starlight is holy to them ever afterwards and why they call themselves the People of the Stars. Something was already hunting in that dark: Melkor took the ones who strayed and made the first orcs of them, the oldest and least comfortable idea in the whole legendarium. The bay was gone before the sun first rose.

name: Dagobah
blurb: A swamp planet with no cities, no technology and a very strong presence in the Force. One resident, who is not accepting visitors.

name: Dakara
blurb: The sacred world where the Jaffa believe their species began, a plain of weathered temples above a device the Ancients left behind that can rewrite all life in a galaxy. Handle carefully.

name: Dale
blurb: A city of bells and toymakers rebuilt out of its own ashes, with the best market between the Mountains and the Sea. Everything is new, everything is bright, and everyone can tell you exactly how long they were homeless.
about: Old Dale was burned by Smaug and stood empty for two centuries; Bard rebuilt it after the Battle of Five Armies with dwarf money and dwarf masons. By the War of the Ring it is rich enough to matter, and it fights its own siege alongside Erebor while everyone in the south is busy — Brand and Dáin both die at the gate, which the book records in a single sentence.

name: Darillium
blurb: Home to the Singing Towers, which sing, and a restaurant with a twenty-four-year night where couples go to say the things they have been putting off. Bring tissues.

name: Death's Domain
blurb: A black garden with black flowers and a very large house, kept by an anthropomorphic personification who is trying hard to understand people and getting closer than most people manage.
about: Death built it himself, working from descriptions, which is why the perspective is slightly wrong everywhere and the fish in the pond are made of bone. He keeps a white horse called Binky, an adopted daughter, a granddaughter and an increasingly complicated interest in humanity. He is not cruel. He is simply the last thing you see, and he takes the job seriously. THERE IS NO JUSTICE. THERE IS JUST ME.

name: Death's Domain — the Ramtops
blurb: The high Ramtops beyond Lancre: bandits, trolls who turn to stone in the heat, dwarf mines, and a monastery of monks who look after history and get it wrong occasionally.
about: The Ramtops run the length of the Disc and get steadily less hospitable the higher you go. The History Monks at Oi Dong slice and store time itself, moving it from places that are not using it — Wednesdays in a quiet village — to places that need more. Lu-Tze, the sweeper, is the most dangerous man on the Disc and has never hit anyone.

name: Deep Space Nine & Bajor
blurb: A recovering world of terraced farms and monasteries, and the Cardassian station above it beside a stable wormhole. The best bar in the quadrant, run by the least trustworthy man in it.

name: Demons Run
blurb: A military asteroid base run by an order of fighting clerics, built around the belief that demons run when a good man goes to war. Impressively fortified, currently between occupants.
tags: a good man goes to war

name: Diagon Alley
blurb: A crooked shopping street reached by tapping the right brick behind a Charing Cross Road pub. Wands, owls, cauldrons, and a bank staffed by goblins who do not care for you.
about: The best single piece of world-building in the books: an entire economy rendered as a shopping trip, with prices, brand names and a queue. Gringotts runs on carts and dragons; Ollivanders has been making wands since 382 BC and the wand chooses the wizard. Knockturn Alley branches off it and is where the plot goes when it needs to get unpleasant.

name: Discovery One
blurb: Two hundred metres of spacecraft with a centrifuge you can jog around, three colleagues in hibernation, a chess partner who never loses, and one red lens that has been listening to every word.
about: The most convincing ship ever filmed, and the quietest: no engine noise, no music, just breathing. HAL is not malfunctioning so much as resolving a contradiction he was given by people who never expected him to notice it, and the pod bay conversation is still the most frightening thing in the genre because it is so polite.

name: District 12
blurb: A coal-mining district at the edge of the map, fenced off, half-starved and largely ignored — which turns out to be the only useful thing about it.
about: The Seam, the Hob black market, the woods beyond an electric fence that is usually switched off for want of power. Collins based it on Appalachian mining towns, and the detail that matters is that hunting outside the fence is illegal but tolerated, because the Peacekeepers also want to eat. The bakery, the meadow and the mockingjays all pay off later, which is why the place is worth walking around.

name: Dol Amroth
blurb: A white castle on a green headland above a warm sea, with knights in swan-winged helms and the only beach holiday in Gondor. The princes here have elvish blood and better manners than anyone in Minas Tirith.
about: Dol Amroth is the one part of Gondor that reads like a holiday: a sea-fief with its own fleet, its own accent and a ruling house said to descend from a marriage with the elves of the vanished haven up the coast. Imrahil brings its swan-knights to the siege of Minas Tirith, and they are the only reinforcements that arrive on time.

name: Dorahl
blurb: A generation ship so vast its people forgot it was a ship, worshipping the reactor as a sun and treating the idea of an outside as heresy. The hull hatch is up a mountain, if you fancy it.

name: Dorne
blurb: Sun, blood oranges and water gardens, run by the only kingdom the dragons never conquered. Relaxed about most things, unforgiving about the rest.

name: Dragonstone
blurb: A black volcanic island carved with dragons, sitting on a mountain of dragonglass. Bleak, dramatic, and the ancestral seat of people who marry their siblings.

name: Dunharrow & the Paths of the Dead
blurb: A cliff refuge reached by a switchback road lined with carved figures nobody can explain, and a door in the mountain that the horses will not go through. The dead do keep their oath, eventually.
about: The Púkel-men on the stair were carved by a people already forgotten when the Rohirrim arrived, and Tolkien leaves them unexplained on purpose. Behind the Dimholt door the Paths run under the Ered Nimrais to the Stone of Erech, where Isildur's oathbreakers have been waiting three thousand years for someone with the right to call them.

name: Dunland
blurb: Wet green hills full of people with a three-hundred-year grievance about who owns Rohan, and they are not entirely wrong. Warm enough welcome, provided you are not blond and on a horse.
about: The Dunlendings were pushed out of Calenardhon when Gondor handed it to Eorl, and have wanted it back ever since, which is why Saruman finds them so easy to recruit. Tolkien gives them a real case and then has Erkenbrand's riders cut them to pieces at the Fords — and afterwards Erkenbrand feeds the prisoners and sends them home, which is as near to a peace settlement as the book gets.

name: Durmstrang
blurb: A castle of four floors somewhere with a great deal of snow, fires lit only for light and warmth, a black lake in front of it, and a ship that surfaces out of the lake when the school goes travelling.
about: Durmstrang is characterised almost entirely by that ship coming up through the bottom of a lake, which is the best entrance in the series. Karkaroff is a coward and a former Death Eater who gave up names to save himself, and the school's habit of teaching curses rather than defence against them is treated by everyone as a continental eccentricity.

name: Earth, the Thirteenth Colony
blurb: The planet at the end of the star map: a radioactive ruin two thousand years dead, found by people who had spent four years praying for it. The bleakest scene in the show, and the best.
about: The Thirteenth Tribe were Cylons, they built a civilisation here, and they destroyed it — which the fleet discovers by walking through the glass. Adama standing in the rubble as the music drops is the series' whole argument: all of this has happened before is not a comfort, it is a warning. They leave, find another planet, and name that one Earth instead.

name: Edoras & Rohan
blurb: A golden hall on a lone hill above endless grass, and the best horses in the world. Come for the riding, stay because someone has taken your horse.

name: Ego
blurb: A planet-sized garden of coloured stone, floating bubbles and perfect symmetry, every inch of it grown by one Celestial who is also the landscape, the weather and — if you stay long enough — you.
about: Ego is the franchise's best bad father: a living planet who built himself a body to go looking for company, seeded a thousand worlds with his own expansion, and killed every child who could not power it. The paradise is genuinely beautiful and the ulterior motive is genuinely there, which is what the film is about.

name: Epsilon III
blurb: The planet under the station: hollow, packed with a million years of machinery, and run by a caretaker who plugged himself into it voluntarily and has never been happier about anything.
about: Draal takes the Great Machine because it needs a living mind to run it, and gets in exchange the ability to see anywhere and lift almost anything. Its builders left it as a defence and it has been waiting ever since — under a planet that Earth surveyed, catalogued and declared uninhabited before parking a quarter of a million people above it.

name: Erebor
blurb: The Lonely Mountain — a dwarf kingdom of vaulted halls and a treasury that has caused two wars. Superb metalwork, excellent ale, occasional dragon.

name: Erudite Headquarters
blurb: Glass, blue clothing, silent reading rooms and the best research facility left in the city, run by people who have concluded that everybody else's ignorance is a solvable problem.
about: Erudite are the villains because they are certain, and the argument underneath the book is that a faction organised entirely around intelligence will eventually decide it ought to be in charge. The library really is magnificent. The serum programme that turns an entire faction into a remote-controlled army is developed two floors below it.
photoTopics: Rows of desks in study hall

name: Ezellohar
blurb: A green mound outside Valimar with two trees on it, one silver and one gold, whose light is the light everything else in the world is a copy of. Best visited before the spider arrives.
about: Telperion and Laurelin lit Aman for millennia in alternating shifts, mingling for an hour twice a day. That light is what Fëanor caught in the Silmarils, which is why Morgoth wanted them and why he came with Ungoliant and drank the Trees dry. The last flower and the last fruit became the Moon and the Sun; everything luminous in Tolkien afterwards is a fragment of this hill.

name: Fangorn Forest
blurb: The oldest forest left standing, and it is watching you. Nothing here is in a hurry, including any conversation you may be invited into.

name: Ferenginar
blurb: A rain-soaked world where commerce is a religion, admission is charged for everything including the temples, and the 285 Rules of Acquisition are studied like scripture.
about: The Ferengi began as an attempt at a menacing new enemy and failed completely, so Deep Space Nine did the sensible thing and made them funny — then, quietly, made them the show's best vehicle for satire about labour, family and unregulated capitalism. It rains 178 days a year and they have seventeen words for rain, none of which is 'rain'.

name: Flatland
blurb: A two-dimensional plane where your class is the number of your sides, fog is a public utility that lets people judge one another accurately, and it rains from the North so everybody knows which way is up.
about: Abbott's satire is not gentle. Flatland's women are straight lines — lethal end-on, legally obliged to sway constantly and to emit a peace-cry on entering a room — and irregular polygons are destroyed at birth for the public good. The Square narrates all of it approvingly, which is the joke, and then spends the second half of the book in prison for having seen a third dimension and said so.

name: Fornost & Annúminas
blurb: Two dead capitals of a kingdom nobody in the south remembers: a hill of grass-grown foundations, and a lake city with its towers still standing in the water.
about: Arnor split, fell to Angmar and stopped being a country in 1974 of the Third Age. The astonishing thing is that its line never ended — the shabby Rangers you meet in the Bree taproom are its remnant, and one of them is the heir. Aragorn rebuilt Annúminas by Lake Evendim and made it a royal seat again, which is the payoff to a background detail a thousand pages old.
photoTopics: Lake and hills still water England

name: Freecloud
blurb: A lawless commercial world of holographic advertising that follows you down the street, where anything is for sale and the only real question is who is currently holding the debt.

name: Gallifrey
blurb: Orange skies, silver-leaved trees and a glass-domed Citadel of Time Lords who watch everything and interfere with nothing, allegedly. Twin suns rise in the south.

name: Gemenon
blurb: The colony that still reads the Sacred Scrolls literally: temples, seminaries, a great deal of scripture, and the school every monotheist terrorist in the story turns out to have attended.
about: Gemenon takes the Scrolls of Pythia as history rather than metaphor — which matters enormously, because by the third season those Scrolls are being read aloud on the bridge as navigation instructions and turn out to be broadly correct. Caprica shows the other half of it: the Soldiers of the One recruiting in Gemenese classrooms.

name: Genua
blurb: A river city of gumbo, voodoo and Mardi Gras, currently being forced into a fairy tale by a godmother who has decided everyone will be happy whether they like it or not.
about: Genua is New Orleans, and Witches Abroad uses it to make a serious point in a silly book: that stories have their own momentum, and someone determined to make life fit one will grind up anybody who does not. Mrs Gogol's voodoo works by belief and gumbo. The food descriptions are the best Pratchett ever wrote.

name: Giedi Prime
blurb: A stripped industrial world under a black sun, seat of House Harkonnen. The architecture is brutal, the entertainments are worse, and there is no natural light anywhere.

name: Godric's Hollow
blurb: A village where wizards and Muggles have lived side by side for centuries: a green with a war memorial that changes while you look at it, a church, a graveyard full of famous names, and one ruined cottage nobody has repaired.
about: The best chapter in Deathly Hallows is a walk around a village on Christmas Eve. Two graves, a memorial that turns into a statue of a family of three, and a house left standing as a monument with a signboard covered in scrawled messages. It is also where Bathilda Bagshot turns out not to be Bathilda Bagshot.

name: Gondolin
blurb: A white city in a ring of mountains, hidden for four hundred years, with the best masons, the best fountains and the worst succession planning of the Elder Days. Nobody who goes in is permitted to leave.
about: Turgon's city stood on a green plain inside the Encircling Mountains, reachable only through a guarded tunnel, and it fell because one man was let out and one man was let in. The Fall of Gondolin was the first story Tolkien ever wrote — in a hospital bed in 1917 — and the last one he was still revising fifty years later.

name: Gont
blurb: A single mountain rising out of the sea, known for goats, goatherds, pirates and wizards. Ged was born on it, and came back to it when everything else was finished.
about: Le Guin opens the first book with Gont and closes the cycle there, which tells you what she thought mattered. The island is poor, steep and cold, and its people are famously taciturn. The mountain is high enough that the villages on its flanks are above the weather; Ogion the Silent walked its paths for years and taught by not speaking, which is the best lesson in the book.

name: Gormenghast
blurb: A castle so vast that whole wings have been forgotten, governed entirely by ritual that nobody understands and nobody may alter. Extraordinary. Suffocating.

name: Gringotts
blurb: A marble banking hall on top of miles of cart track, hundreds of fathoms down, where the vaults get older and worse the further you go and there is a blind dragon chained beneath the oldest of them.
about: Goblin banking is the sharpest thing in the books and the most argued over: a people who have been robbed by wizards for centuries, hold all their money, and take the opposite view of who owns what. The security is genuinely good — the Thief's Downfall, the Gemino curse, and a dragon conditioned to flinch at a hand-held rattle.

name: Hala
blurb: The Kree capital: a blue-skinned empire, a Supreme Intelligence that appears to you wearing the face of whoever you most admire, and a sky that has been going out ever since somebody unplugged it.
about: Hala runs on conquest and on an artificial intelligence that speaks to each citizen in the shape of the person they respected most — which is how you get a civilisation that only ever agrees with itself. Captain Marvel spends one film being told she is Kree and the next on a Hala with no sun, no water and a thoroughly earned grudge.

name: Harad
blurb: Spice markets, red silk, war-elephants the size of houses, and an old, deep and entirely reasonable dislike of Gondor. The books never take you here, which tells you who is holding the pen.
about: The Haradrim are the enemy the story never troubles to understand, and Tolkien knew it: the one moment he gives them is Sam looking at a dead southron and wondering what lies he was told to bring him so far from home. The mûmakil are real and enormous. Númenor colonised these coasts and was hated for it, and Sauron simply inherited the grudge and put it to work.

name: Helium, Barsoom
blurb: Twin cities of scarlet and yellow towers above the ochre moss of a dying Mars, with flying ships, four-armed green warriors and a princess who needs no rescuing.

name: Helm's Deep
blurb: A fortress wedged into a ravine that has never fallen while men defended it. Spectacular walls, dramatic acoustics, and a strong chance of being asked to hold a line.

name: Highgarden
blurb: Terraced gardens, orchards and the richest farmland in the Seven Kingdoms. The food is the best in the world and so is the poisoning.

name: Himring
blurb: A bare cold hill with a fortress on it that never fell, held by the least forgivable of the sons of Fëanor. Bracing views, iron discipline, and a host under an oath that will make him do terrible things.
about: Maedhros held the eastern march from Himring for four hundred years, and it was the one stronghold to survive the Battle of Sudden Flame. He is the most sympathetic Fëanorian — rescued from Thangorodrim missing a hand, gave up the high kingship, and still went on to sack Doriath and the Havens over an oath he could not put down. The hill outlived Beleriand; it is an island now.

name: Hogsmeade
blurb: Britain's only entirely wizarding village: thatched cottages under snow, butterbeer at the Three Broomsticks, and a pub down the road that nobody sensible drinks in.
about: Third-years and above may visit on scheduled weekends, which makes it the closest thing the books have to a holiday destination. Honeydukes has a secret passage in its cellar; the Shrieking Shack is the most haunted building in Britain and is not haunted at all. Butterbeer, invented for the page and later made real by a theme park, is somewhere between cream soda and a hot toddy.

name: Hogwarts
blurb: A thousand-year-old castle of moving staircases, portraits with opinions and a lake with a squid in it. Muggles see a ruin with warning signs. Term begins on 1 September.
about: Four founders, four houses, and a building that actively resists mapping — 142 staircases, some of which go somewhere different on Fridays. The teaching is uneven, the safety record is appalling and the food is superb. The Room of Requirement appears only when you need it; the Forbidden Forest is forbidden for good reasons that nobody enforces. Filming used Alnwick Castle, Durham and Gloucester Cathedrals and Glenfinnan Viaduct, all of which you can actually visit.

name: Holy Terra
blurb: A planet-wide hive city built over the bones of Earth, centred on a golden throne that consumes a thousand psykers a day. Pilgrimage of a lifetime; do not look up.

name: Hoth
blurb: An ice planet with nothing to recommend it except that nobody looks for you here. Night temperatures will kill an unprotected human in minutes.

name: Hyrule
blurb: Green fields and a ruined castle in the middle distance, with a shrine on every horizon and something worth climbing behind it. Bring a paraglider and a great many apples.
about: Hyrule is rebuilt from scratch almost every game — the same kingdom, the same princess, the same sword, a different map. Breath of the Wild's version put the whole thing on one continuous terrain with no loading and a rule that anything you can see, you can walk to, which is the clearest statement of intent in the medium. Miyamoto has said the original came from remembering exploring hillsides and caves as a boy near Kyoto.

name: Isengard
blurb: A ring of stone around a black tower, once a garden and a library, now a pit of forges and felled trees. The wizard inside has a mind of metal and wheels.
about: Orthanc itself was built by the Númenóreans and cannot be broken — everything Saruman did to it was landscaping. The valley was wooded and beautiful before he cut it down for fuel, which is precisely why the Ents come, and why the book's most satisfying scene is a river being let back in.

name: Isla Nublar
blurb: A tropical island theme park stocked with de-extincted dinosaurs and a security system with a single point of failure. Spared no expense. Should have spared some.

name: Isla Sorna
blurb: The factory floor: the island where the animals were actually grown before being shipped to the park, evacuated in a hurry after a hurricane and left to run itself for six years. No fences, no paddocks, no staff.
about: Site B is the better idea. Nublar is a theme park that fails; Sorna is an ecosystem that succeeded without anybody watching, which is what makes The Lost World's premise worth the sequel. The animals bred, the lysine contingency did nothing, and the survey team arrive to find an island that has stopped being an experiment and become a place.

name: Ithilien
blurb: The garden of Gondor gone feral — olive, bay and terebinth growing over abandoned terraces, rabbit stewed with herbs, and an enemy border two valleys east.
about: Tolkien spends pages here on the smell of crushed leaves precisely because it is the last green thing before Mordor. Faramir's rangers keep a lodging behind the waterfall at Henneth Annûn and blindfold anyone they bring in. After the war it was cleared and made a princedom, which is as close as the book comes to a happy ending for a landscape.

name: Ithilien & Osgiliath
blurb: The garden of Gondor gone to seed — herbs growing wild over abandoned terraces, and downriver the broken bridges of a city that was the jewel of the kingdom.
about: Tolkien loved Ithilien best of anywhere he invented, and it shows: the chapter set there is mostly a list of plants. It is the one place in the book where the war is close enough to hear and the prose still stops to notice tamarisk and marjoram. Osgiliath below it was the old capital, fought over so many times that nobody lives there any more.

name: Jakku
blurb: A junkyard planet where a fleet came to die. Scavenging is the entire economy and portions are paid in something that expands into bread.

name: Jurassic World
blurb: The park that opened, ran for ten years and took twenty thousand visitors a day: a main street, a monorail, a lagoon with something enormous in it, and a corporate need for a bigger attraction every few seasons.
about: Jurassic World's joke is that a functioning dinosaur park would be boring within a decade, so the marketing department commissions a hybrid — and the hybrid is smarter than the marketing department. Everything about the resort is convincingly mundane: the queue times, the sponsored enclosures, the gift shop selling the animal that eats the tourists.

name: Justice World
blurb: A prison station with a field that reflects any crime straight back onto whoever commits it. Punch someone and you break your own nose. Superb public order. No fun whatsoever.
about: A proper science-fiction idea inside a sitcom: a penal colony that needs no guards because harm becomes self-administering. It also puts Rimmer on trial for killing the entire crew, a charge he insists on pleading guilty to out of sheer vanity, and the court's eventual verdict is the kindest assessment anyone ever gives him.

name: Kaer Morhen
blurb: A half-ruined fortress up a mountain trail nobody maintains, where witchers are made and, in winter, where the last handful of them come home to drink and repair their swords.
about: The Trial of the Grasses killed most of the boys put through it and can no longer be performed, because the keep was sacked and the mutagens destroyed — which means the witchers are a profession with no new entrants and a known end date. That elegiac note is the whole series in one building. The winter sequences here, with four monster hunters cooking badly and arguing, are the warmest thing Sapkowski wrote.

name: Kamar-Taj
blurb: A courtyard behind an unmarked door in Kathmandu where they teach you to fold a city, open a doorway to anywhere, and read six dead languages. Tea is provided. The library is the dangerous part.
about: The MCU's one school, and its best joke is that the librarian is the real authority: sanctums, sling rings, and a man who has lost colleagues to stolen books. The Ancient One's entire syllabus is a long campaign to persuade a brilliant surgeon that he is not the most important person in any given room.

name: Kamino
blurb: An ocean world of permanent storm where a tall, courteous people grow armies to order in white sterile halls raised above the waves on stilts.
about: Kamino was deleted from the star charts by someone who did not want it found, which is how a clone army got built without the Republic noticing. Visually it is the cleanest thing in Star Wars — all white curves and rain — and the contrast with what it manufactures is the whole idea. The Kaminoans are unfailingly polite about it.

name: Karn
blurb: A volcanic world of black rock and a Sacred Flame tended by the Sisterhood, whose Elixir of Life will fix anything, at a price, and whose ship-wrecking mind-powers explain the debris field.

name: Kashyyyk
blurb: Wroshyr trees kilometres tall with cities built in the canopy, and a warrior culture of very large people who take debts extremely seriously.

name: Kaylon 1
blurb: A machine world of immaculate order, built on the mass graves of the organic species that made it. Spotless, silent, and constantly evaluating whether your existence is justified.

name: King's Landing
blurb: A million people, a Red Keep, and a smell you never fully stop noticing. The politics are magnificent and the life expectancy of anyone interesting is short.

name: Knowhere
blurb: A mining colony drilled into the severed head of a dead Celestial, where the bone is real estate, the brain tissue is the export, and a bar fight is included in the price of the ticket.
about: Knowhere is the best set-piece idea the Guardians films have: a frontier town inside a skull, run by a collector, lit like a casino and mined for organic matter that is technically somebody's remains. It gets bought outright later and turned into a home, which is a lot of retail activity for one severed head.

name: Kobol
blurb: The world all twelve colonies came from, abandoned two thousand years ago and left to the forest — an opera house in ruins, a tomb full of stars, and scripture that turns out to be directions.

name: Lake-town
blurb: A timber town standing on posts in a lake, kept afloat by the barrel trade and a certain flexibility about who is in charge. The old town is still down there under the water. So is the dragon.
about: Esgaroth lives off the wine and barrel traffic between Dorwinion and the wood-elves, which is exactly how the dwarves get out of Thranduil's cells. The Master is a coward and an embezzler and Tolkien plainly enjoys writing him. Bard shoots Smaug from the burning town and then leads the survivors upriver to refound Dale — the only disaster relief effort in the legendarium that works.

name: Laputa
blurb: A flying island of mathematicians and musicians so lost in abstraction they need servants to flap their ears when it is their turn to speak. The view is remarkable. The conversation is not.

name: Las Vegas, 2049
blurb: An abandoned city under orange radioactive dust, with statues, a working jukebox, a hologram of Elvis performing to an empty theatre, and exactly one resident who would rather not be found.
about: The best sequence in 2049: Villeneuve and Deakins shot the ruined city in solid orange light, and it is silent except for a bee. The bee is the point — nothing is alive out here, so a bee means somebody is keeping them. Deckard has been hiding in a casino for thirty years with a dog whose realness he declines to confirm.

name: Lilliput
blurb: An island empire of people six inches high, currently at war with Blefuscu over which end of an egg to open. Charming for an afternoon; the politics are exhausting.

name: Lineland
blurb: A single line on which everyone is a point or a segment, your two neighbours are the only beings you will ever perceive, and the King cannot be brought to understand that sideways exists.
about: The Square visits Lineland in a dream and tries to explain width to a monarch who has never had a neighbour he was not touching. He fails, loses his temper, and is threatened with violence for heresy — which is precisely what happens to him one chapter later, when the Sphere does exactly the same thing to him. The structure is the argument.
photoTopics: Row of posts in a line

name: Lockwood Manor
blurb: A gothic house full of natural history: panelled halls, a fossil collection, a granddaughter with an unusual medical history, and an auction in the basement selling live animals to arms dealers.
about: Fallen Kingdom relocates the franchise indoors and it works far better than it should — a haunted-house third act with a raptor in the corridors and a bidding war underneath it. The house is also where the series finally says the quiet part: the value of these animals was never scientific, and the buyers were always going to be military.

name: Logopolis
blurb: A quiet stone city where mathematicians mutter numbers that hold the universe together. Do not interrupt them, do not raise your voice, and do not touch anything.

name: Los Angeles 2019
blurb: Permanent night, permanent rain, two hundred storeys of advertising, and a noodle bar where you ask for four and are given two. The best-looking city ever filmed and a genuinely terrible place to live.
about: Scott's Los Angeles is the most copied image in science fiction: neon signage, umbrellas with lit handles, and rain that never stops. Everyone who could afford to leave has gone off-world, so what is left is corporations, street food and a language four tongues deep. The city is doing the film's arguing for it — nothing green, nothing alive, everything sold.

name: Los Angeles, 2029
blurb: A city of rubble and skulls under permanent ash cloud, worked over by hunter-killers on searchlights. Humans move at night, in small groups, without lights. Daylight belongs to the machines.
about: Cameron gives this maybe ninety seconds a film and it is the most influential ninety seconds in the genre: blue light, tank treads crushing a skull, tracer fire. The restraint is deliberate — everything you know about 2029 you learn from a traumatised soldier describing it badly in the back of a stolen car in 1984.

name: Lothlórien
blurb: Golden mallorn woods where time runs differently and everyone speaks in a way that makes you feel underdressed. You will leave with gifts and an unresolved feeling.

name: Lyra's Oxford
blurb: Oxford as it is in a world with airships, anbaric light and everyone's soul walking beside them as an animal. Jordan College has a roof you are not supposed to be on.
about: Pullman's Oxford is the real one with the Reformation gone the other way: the Church runs the sciences under the name of experimental theology, and the colleges are its rivals. Dæmons settle into a fixed animal form at adolescence, which is the series' most quietly devastating idea — you find out what you are, and then you are it. The alethiometer, a truth-telling instrument read with three needles and a book of symbols, is the plot's engine.

name: Magrathea
blurb: A planet that manufactures other planets to order, currently in recession and asleep for five million years. Ask to see the fjords. They won an award.

name: Malcassairo
blurb: The last planet, a hundred trillion years on, where the stars have gone out and the last humans queue for a rocket to somewhere called Utopia that may not be there.

name: Mars Colony
blurb: Pressure domes, red dust, tunnels, and a resistance movement that everyone on Earth calls terrorism and everyone on Mars calls the reason the water supply works at all.
about: Mars is Babylon 5's Earth problem in miniature: a colony run for the benefit of a homeworld, then bombed by it when President Clark needs an example made. Free Mars runs through the whole series as the thing Earth would rather not talk about, and in the end Mars gets its independence written into the peace.

name: Meereen
blurb: A pyramid city of coloured brick on a hot bay, mid-revolution and unsure how it feels about that. Fighting pits, harpies, and a queen with dragons.

name: Menegroth
blurb: The Thousand Caves: a forest carved in stone, inside a wood held shut by the enchantment of a Maia queen. The wine is old and so is everyone drinking it.
about: Melian's Girdle kept Doriath safe for centuries — until Thingol invited dwarves in to set a Silmaril in a necklace and then argued with them about the fee. He is killed over it, the Girdle fails, and the kingdom is sacked twice by people who were meant to be on its side. The clearest lesson in the legendarium about what a beautiful object does to whoever owns it.

name: Menzoberranzan
blurb: A drow city carved into stalagmites two miles below the surface, lit by faerie fire, ruled by matriarchs, and organised entirely around murdering your way up the house rankings.
about: The Underdark is a lightless continent under the continent, and Menzoberranzan is its most famous city: eight noble houses in permanent lethal competition, held in check by a goddess who approves of the competition. Salvatore's Drizzt Do'Urden left it, which is the whole point of the character. The architecture — spun stone, glowing sculpture, cathedral-scale caverns — is the most striking thing in the setting.

name: Midnight
blurb: A planet of solid diamond under a sun whose light kills anything it touches, viewed from sealed leisure buses. Objectively spectacular, and something out there learns to speak by copying you.

name: Milliways
blurb: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe, where you dine while the cosmos collapses outside the window, twice nightly. Pay by depositing a penny in your own era.

name: Minas Morgul
blurb: A beautiful white city lit from the inside by a corpse-light, in a flowering valley that smells of rot. Every window is open. Nothing that looks out of them is anyone you want to meet.
about: It was Minas Ithil, the Tower of the Rising Moon, and Gondor built it to watch Mordor. The Nazgûl took it in 2002 of the Third Age and have held it since. The flowers in the valley are Tolkien's own detail — beautiful and yet horrible of shape, like the demented forms in an uneasy dream — and the road out of the city climbs the stairs towards Shelob.

name: Minas Tirith
blurb: Seven white tiers built into a mountainside, with a view across the Pelennor and a great deal of stairs. Magnificent, ceremonial, and periodically besieged.

name: Minbar
blurb: A cold world of crystal cities that sing when the wind crosses them, run by a caste system of workers, warriors and religious, none of whom will give you a straight answer about anything.

name: Miranda
blurb: A terraformed world of thirty million, left off every star chart. The cities are intact, the power still runs, and everyone lay down and stopped. Something in the air made them stop.

name: Mirkwood
blurb: Sixty leagues of black woodland with one path through it, and the path is the good news. Do not leave it, do not drink the water, do not follow the lights, and do not on any account fall asleep.
about: It was Greenwood the Great until a shadow settled at Dol Guldur in the south and turned it — the Necromancer there being, as it turns out, Sauron. The spiders are his overspill. After the war the wood was cleansed and renamed Eryn Lasgalen, and the elves and the Beornings divided it between them, which is the tidiest ending in the Appendices.

name: Moclus
blurb: A single-sex industrial world and the Union's main weapons supplier, run on discipline, forges and an official position on gender that the rest of the galaxy finds increasingly hard to sit next to.

name: Mordor
blurb: A volcanic plain of ash and slag under a permanent overcast, ringed by mountains and administered with real commitment. Remarkably quiet in the off-season.

name: Moria
blurb: The greatest dwarf-realm ever delved, now empty except for what moved in afterwards. Astonishing halls. Do not go alone, at night, or at all.

name: Mos Eisley Spaceport
blurb: You will never find a more wretched hive of scum and villainy. Outstanding live music, and the drinks are cheap because the clientele are unlikely to complain.

name: Mustafar
blurb: A world of open lava rivers and mining platforms, where the air is unbreathable and the ground is optional. Historically a poor choice of duelling venue.

name: Naboo
blurb: Lakeside palaces, waterfall cities and rolling green hills, with an entire amphibian civilisation in the planet's core. The most beautiful world in the galaxy and it knows it.

name: Nargothrond
blurb: A fortress-city hollowed into a river cliff, secret for four hundred years and ruined in an afternoon by good advice ignored and a bridge built out of pride. There is a dragon in the treasury now.
about: Finrod built it and gave up his crown to keep a promise. Túrin then talked its people out of secrecy and into open war and a great stone bridge, which is exactly how Glaurung's army walked in. The dragon sat on the hoard afterwards and broke the mind of everyone who came looking — the darkest thread Tolkien wrote, and the one closest to a Norse saga.

name: Narn
blurb: A world stripped to bedrock by a century of Centauri occupation, rebuilt by a people who remember every day of it. Harsh, proud, deeply religious, and not remotely interested in forgiving.

name: Neverland
blurb: An island of pirates, mermaids and lost boys where nobody grows up and the crocodile has swallowed a clock. Endless adventure, and you will forget your parents' faces.

name: New Caprica
blurb: A cold, marginal world hidden inside a nebula, settled by a fleet that could not keep running. Tent city, thin soil, one year of hard-won ordinary life, and then the ships came back.

name: New Earth
blurb: Humanity's replacement Earth, five billion years on, with apple grass on the hills above New New York — the fifteenth city of that name, and nobody counts the first fourteen.

name: New York City
blurb: The real New York, plus a mansion school in Westchester, a sanctum on Bleecker Street, a tower with an A on it, and property damage nobody's insurance covers.
about: Marvel's founding decision was to put superheroes in a real city with real streets rather than an invented Gotham or Metropolis, so that Peter Parker could worry about rent in Queens. The consequence is that Manhattan has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times, is under regular alien invasion, and remains the most desirable real estate in fiction. The Sanctum Sanctorum's address, 177A Bleecker Street, is a real corner.

name: Nidavellir
blurb: A forge the size of a solar system built in a ring around a dying star, worked by dwarves who make weapons for gods and have been sitting in the dark since the last customer had them all killed.
about: Infinity War's one piece of pure spectacle: a ring larger than a planet, a neutron star restarted by hand, and the last dwarf standing in a workshop full of his family's absence. Eitri made Mjolnir and he made the Gauntlet, which leaves him responsible for a remarkable amount of the plot in both directions.

name: Nimbus III
blurb: A shared Federation-Klingon-Romulan colony founded to prove three empires could cooperate. Twenty years on it is a dust bowl with one bar, called Paradise City, ironically.

name: Novigrad
blurb: The Continent's biggest free city — docks, banks, brothels, bathhouses and a religious purge in progress. Mages are being burned in the square; business continues.
about: Sapkowski's world is one where the fantastical is being squeezed out by politics, and Novigrad is where you watch it happen: the Eternal Fire's witch hunts are less about theology than about who owns the mage-run banks. Everything is for sale, including the guard. The card game Gwent, invented as flavour, became popular enough to be released as its own product.

name: Nurn
blurb: Mordor's breadbasket: irrigated fields around a bitter inland sea, worked by slaves, feeding the armies. Grim, fertile, and startlingly ordinary for the address.
about: Armies have to eat, and Tolkien did not forget it: the great slave-worked fields around the Sea of Núrnen are what make Mordor a country rather than a monster's lair. Nurn is also the site of the war's quietest good decision — Aragorn freed the land and gave it outright to the people who had been farming it, which is the only land reform in the legendarium.

name: Oldtown & the Citadel
blurb: The oldest city in Westeros, and the Citadel where maesters forge their chains. The library is the best in the known world, and they will not let you take anything out.

name: Organia
blurb: An unremarkable pastoral village of placid peasants who have not changed in millennia, sitting on a strategically vital world. They are not peasants, and they will end your war for you.

name: Orodruin
blurb: Mount Doom: a cinder cone with a road up it, a chamber cut into its side, and the only fire in the world hot enough to unmake the Ring. Nothing else to see, and everyone goes anyway.
about: The Sammath Naur is the place the entire book walks towards, and when Frodo finally stands in it he fails — he claims the Ring, and it is Gollum's greed and a misplaced foot that finish the errand. Tolkien thought that the point: the quest is completed by a mercy shown years earlier, not by anybody's strength of will.

name: Ossiriand
blurb: Seven rivers, elm woods, and elves who dress in green, sing constantly and will not be seen unless they choose to be. No towns, no roads, no metal, and the finest autumn in Arda.
about: The Green-elves were the least interested of anybody in the wars, which is why Beren and Lúthien went there to live out their second and final life in peace. The Ents were in these woods too — Tolkien has them come down to help the elves against the dwarves, the one place where the two ideas touch. When Beleriand drowned, a strip of Ossiriand survived as Lindon.

name: Pahvo
blurb: An untouched forest world where every living thing vibrates in harmony and the whole planet hums one continuous chord. The inhabitants are the sound. They would like everyone to get along.

name: Pandora
blurb: A moon of bioluminescent rainforest, floating mountains and a planet-wide neural network. The air will kill you in four minutes and the wildlife will get there first.

name: Peladon
blurb: A cold mountain kingdom of superstition and mining strikes, arguing itself into the Galactic Federation while a sacred beast called Aggedor may or may not still stalk the tunnels.

name: Pelargir
blurb: Gondor's great river-haven: shipyards, salt air, ten miles of quay, and a corsair problem that was eventually solved by hiring the dead.
about: Pelargir was the port of the Faithful before Gondor existed, and it is where Aragorn brings the Oathbreakers ashore to take the corsair fleet — the hour the war stops being lost. The reinforcements that turn the Pelennor sail up the Anduin from here, which is why the black ships coming into view are the most frightening thing Minas Tirith sees all day.

name: Persephone
blurb: A border world of grand estates and open-air docks, where the wealthy hold masked balls uphill and everyone else works the shipyards downhill. Good place to pick up work you shouldn't take.

name: Picon
blurb: The Colonial Fleet's home water: island cities, deep anchorages, the Academy every pilot passes through, and the headquarters that was gone before anyone understood there was a war.
about: Picon is the sea colony — Fleet HQ, the Academy, and enough coastline that the whole culture is boats. It also took the opening strike of the war: Picon Fleet Headquarters was hit first, which is why what survives of the Colonial Fleet is one museum piece and forty raptors.

name: Pointland
blurb: A single point containing one being who is his own universe, his own subjects and his own applause, and who cannot be told otherwise because there is no otherwise. Nothing to see. Nobody to meet.
about: The Sphere shows the Square the abyss of no dimensions as a warning. The Point is perfectly happy, praises himself in his own voice, and treats any speech from outside as one of his own thoughts — so he cannot be corrected, argued with, or humbled. It is the book's coldest joke: the lowest being in the hierarchy is the only one who cannot be humiliated.
