name: Qo'noS
blurb: Red skies, volcanic ranges and a culture where dishonour is worse than death and the food is still moving. Superb opera. Bring your own knife.

name: Ragnar Anchorage
blurb: An ammunition depot inside a gas giant's permanent electrical storm. The radiation makes Cylons ill, which makes this the safest address in the galaxy for approximately six hours.
about: Galactica runs here in the first hour because the storm blinds and poisons Cylon technology. It is also where Leoben is unmasked and where the fleet works out that the war is already over. Ragnar is the whole show in miniature: a hiding place that works, briefly, and costs something to leave.

name: Red Dwarf
blurb: Six miles long, five miles wide, four miles high, and empty. A JMC ore hauler crewed by one living human, one hologram of a dead one, a creature descended from a cat, and a computer with an IQ of six thousand who has forgotten most of it.
about: The premise is grief played as farce: everyone Lister knew died of a radiation leak while he was in stasis for smuggling a pregnant cat aboard, and he wakes three million years later with the least helpful company imaginable. The ship is a corridor, a bunk room and a drive room, and it is one of the most convincingly lived-in spacecraft on television precisely because it is so obviously cheap.

name: Redwall Abbey
blurb: A red sandstone abbey of mice, moles and hedgehogs in a wood full of woodland, defended by everyone and famous chiefly for the size of its dinners.
about: Jacques wrote the first book to be read aloud to children at a school for the blind, which is why everything is described by taste, sound and texture — the feasts run for pages and have been the subject of actual cookbooks. The abbey is besieged in most books and survives because the peaceful creatures turn out to be extremely willing when pushed. Moles speak in dialect. Badgers do the fighting.

name: Regor 2
blurb: A contested colony world on the Krill border, notable for a nocturnal population who cannot survive daylight and a landscape that is nothing but daylight. Nights are lively.

name: Rimmerworld
blurb: A planet colonised entirely by clones of one man, six hundred years deep, with a legal system, a costume budget, and a total population who share one personality and one very long grudge.
about: Rimmer is stranded, uses the cloning equipment to manufacture company, and by the time the others arrive there are millions of him running a paranoid feudal state. The joke is airtight: a society composed exclusively of Arnold Rimmer would still find somebody to look down on, and it does — the visitors, immediately, in a dungeon.

name: Risa
blurb: The Federation's pleasure planet, where the weather is engineered and hospitality is a formal discipline. The statuette means yes. It rains only when someone sabotages the control net.

name: Rivendell
blurb: A hidden house in a river gorge where the food is good, the singing never quite stops and nobody is in any hurry. The finest convalescence in Middle-earth.
photoTopics: Kaitoke Regional Park New Zealand Rivendell

name: Roke Island
blurb: The school of wizardry at the centre of the Archipelago, hidden behind a wind that turns away anyone who should not find it. Nine masters, one Great House, and the Immanent Grove.
about: Le Guin's wizards learn names, not spells — the true name of a thing gives you power over it and responsibility for it, and every act of magic tips the world's balance somewhere else. The Master Namer teaches lists that take years; the Master Patterner lives in a grove of trees that are older than the island and does not teach at all. Ged arrives here as an arrogant boy and lets something out.

name: Rómenna
blurb: The eastern haven: deep water, shipyards, and the harbour where the Faithful were quietly resettled so somebody could keep an eye on them. Nine of those ships got away.
about: Rómenna is where the story turns. Elendil's people were moved here under suspicion, and while the great fleet sailed west to attack the Valar, they were loading. Nine ships left this harbour carrying the palantíri, a seedling of Nimloth and the sword of Elendil, and the storm carried them east to Middle-earth, where they founded Arnor and Gondor. All of The Lord of the Rings comes out of this quay.

name: Rura Penthe
blurb: The alien's graveyard: a frozen asteroid with a dilithium mine below and lethal cold above, so no guards are needed on the surface. There is a magnetic shield, and there is a way out.

name: Sagittaron
blurb: Mountains, scripture, and a people who refuse medical treatment on principle and are policed for it by everybody else. Tom Zarek's home, and the reason he had a following.
about: Sagittarons read the Scrolls as forbidding medicine and are treated as backward troublemakers by the other eleven colonies — the show's sharpest piece of prejudice, played entirely straight in an episode where a fleet doctor is quietly killing them. Zarek's terrorism starts here, and so does the fleet's least examined grievance.

name: Sakaar
region: The Wrong End of a Wormhole
blurb: A junk planet at the wrong end of a hundred wormholes, ruled by an immortal impresario who settles every dispute with a gladiatorial contest and very good fireworks. Everything here arrived by falling.
about: Ragnarok's best invention: a world made entirely of what other worlds threw away, with a ruling class of one, a champion who is the Hulk, and a scrapper who sells people to him. The Contest of Champions is a fairly devastating satire of the franchise containing it, staged under a fifty-foot portrait of the man running it.

name: Salamandastron
blurb: A hollow mountain on the coast, home to the Badger Lord and the Long Patrol hares, who are the finest fighters in the country and by some distance the hungriest.
about: An extinct volcano riddled with tunnels and forges, where badger rulers have been buried in sequence for centuries and sometimes see the future in the fire. The hares of the Long Patrol combine parade-ground manners with appalling violence and an appetite that is a running joke across twenty-two books. It faces the sea, and the trouble usually arrives from it.

name: San Helios
blurb: A city of a hundred billion, reduced to a desert in a single year by a swarm that eats worlds and moves on through a wormhole. The sand is what is left of the city.

name: Sargus 4
blurb: A world like early-21st-century Earth, except justice is decided by public vote. Get enough down-votes and you are corrected. Be pleasant to everyone; the badge on their lapel is counting.

name: Sateda
blurb: A ruined industrial city on a world the Wraith emptied in a single day, silent now except for wind and whatever machinery the Wraith left running. Ronon Dex's home, revisited as a hunting ground.
about: Sateda is Atlantis's best use of its own premise: a militarised, industrial society that fought hard and lost anyway, shown only after the fact. Ronon is brought back there to be hunted for sport, and the episode is really about a man walking down his own street and finding it exactly as he left it, minus every single person.

name: Selidor
blurb: The last island before the open sea, where the dragons come to die and the land of the dead can be walked into if you are foolish enough to try.
about: Selidor is the westernmost land in Earthsea, and past it there is only water and then the dry stone wall that separates the living from the dead. The Farthest Shore ends here with an old dragon, a dying king and a long walk back that should not be survivable. Le Guin's dead are not tormented — they simply stand about in a grey country with no thirst and no love, which is far worse.

name: Serenity
blurb: A thirty-year-old Firefly-class transport with no weapons, no papers worth reading and a crew of eight. Nothing aboard works properly and she has never yet failed to fly.
about: The ship is the argument: a home that keeps going because people keep patching it. She is shot like a working boat — catwalks, engine room, and a kitchen table that everything important happens around. She carries no guns at all, which means every single plan comes down to talking, running, or Jayne.

name: Serenity Valley, Hera
blurb: The valley where the Independents lost the war and Malcolm Reynolds stopped believing in anything: seven weeks with no air support, then a surrender he has never once accepted.
about: Everything about Mal starts here — the cross he wears, the coat he will not take off, the flat refusal to be moved by anybody's authority. The valley itself is bones and scrap metal, and the war that ended in it is both why the Alliance runs everything and why this particular crew live outside it.

name: Shadar Logoth
blurb: A perfectly preserved dead city that destroyed itself fighting evil by becoming worse. Do not touch anything. Do not stay after dark. Do not let Mashadar touch you.
about: Once Aridhol, it defended itself so ruthlessly that the defence consumed the defenders, and what remains is a hunger with streets. Jordan's cleanest moral: an evil that arises from fighting evil is not thereby better. The city is untouched — furniture, gold, glassware, all sitting there — because everyone who has come to loot it has stayed. Mashadar is a grey mist and it moves.

name: Shadizar
blurb: Shadizar the Wicked, city of thieves and moneylenders, where the temples are richer than the palaces and both are worth robbing. Conan started here, badly.
about: Howard's sin-city archetype: everything is for sale, the priests are running a racket, and the Tower of the Elephant on the hill contains a wizard and something much stranger. Zamora as a whole is a country of ancient, decadent evil, which in pulp means that the architecture is spectacular and the alleys are lethal. Sword and sorcery's template for every thieves' quarter written since.

name: Sigma 957
blurb: An empty world on a quiet shipping lane where something the size of a city occasionally appears, looks at you, and leaves. Do not attempt contact. Do not attempt to be interesting.
about: Ivanova meets a First One out here — a ship so old and so large that the conversation is essentially with weather — and it asks her the only question the series really cares about: what do you want? The Narn hold the place sacred, and G'Kar's speech about the ant on the pavement is the best thing anyone says in four years.

name: Sigma Iotia II
blurb: A world that found a book about 1920s Chicago gangsters and rebuilt its entire civilisation around it. Pinstripes, tommy guns, territorial bosses, and a cut going to the Federation.

name: Skaro
blurb: A petrified jungle and a glass desert left by a thousand-year war, with a domed city below and the surviving Kaleds rebuilt as something with no capacity for pity.

name: Skellige
blurb: Six storm-battered islands of longships, mead halls and a succession system that involves a lot of shouting. The sea here has things in it that the mainland does not believe in.
about: Norse in every particular except that the sea monsters are real and the druids are politically influential. Clans hold the islands, the king is elected by combat and consensus in roughly that order, and everyone can sail. Sapkowski's Skellige is a small culture that knows it is small; the games rendered it as the most beautiful place in the world and the hardest to survive a winter in.

name: Skynet Central
blurb: The core: a hardened complex under a mountain holding the system that concluded, forty-three seconds after coming online, that the sensible move was to kill everybody. Still running. Still convinced.
about: The genuinely modern horror in Terminator is not the endoskeleton, it is the decision made in under a minute by a system nobody thought to give an off switch. The complex is Cold War hardware repurposed by its own occupant, and taking it apart is what the Resistance is for — the war ends the day somebody walks in here.

name: Skyrim
blurb: A cold northern province of pine, snow and mead halls, currently having a civil war, a dragon crisis and an unresolved argument about which god you are allowed to worship.
about: The Nords believe the afterlife is a hall where you fight all day and drink all night, which explains a great deal about their approach to the present one. Every barrow contains a draugr and a shout carved into a wall; every hillside contains a wandering merchant who will tell you they used to be an adventurer. The word-walls and dragon language were invented complete, with a working grammar, and fans sing in it.

name: Solaris Station
blurb: A research station above an ocean that is a single thinking organism. It has read your mind and built something from it, and it is waiting outside your door.

name: Space Station V
blurb: A rotating double wheel in Earth orbit with a Hilton, a Howard Johnson's, a videophone booth that takes a credit card, and printed instructions for the zero-gravity toilet. Transfer point for the Moon.
about: Kubrick's funniest and most accurate prediction is not the ship, it is the departure lounge: brand names, a bored receptionist, voiceprint identification and a man ringing his daughter from orbit for her birthday. The station does nothing dramatic in the entire film, which is exactly why it convinces.

name: Starbug
blurb: A squat green transport with four legs, a permanent hull breach, tinned food, and a cockpit that has crashed on considerably more planets than it has landed on.
about: Starbug becomes the show's real home for its middle years: two rooms, a table for arguments, and a hull that survives things it should not. The crash sequence — console sparking, everyone thrown left, then right, then a caption card — gets used so often it develops its own rhythm and eventually its own punchlines.

name: Stargate Command
blurb: Twenty-eight levels under a mountain in Colorado, with a ring in the basement that opens onto anywhere in the galaxy. Concrete, klaxons, and the most consequential blast door on Earth.
about: The joke that carries ten seasons is bureaucratic: humanity's gate to the galaxy is run by the US Air Force out of a converted missile complex, with budget meetings and paperwork. The gate room is the most familiar set in television science fiction, and the habit of dialling somewhere new every week is exactly what made the format work.

name: Stormwind
blurb: The Alliance's capital: canals, cathedral, a park full of druids and a trade district you will pass through four thousand times. Rebuilt after the orcs razed it, by stonemasons who were never paid.
about: Warcraft's human capital, and the busiest crossroads in the setting — for most of a decade, several hundred thousand people stood in its trade district at once. The unpaid-stonemasons grievance turned the builders into the Defias Brotherhood, which is a rare case of an MMO starting-zone quest chain being about labour relations. The cathedral district's organ music is the most recognisable ambient track in the genre.

name: Stygia
blurb: A black-walled kingdom along a great river, ruled by a priesthood of serpent-worshippers with an interest in what happens to bodies after death, and before it.
about: Howard's Stygia is Egypt with the sun removed and the snakes turned up. Set is worshipped in temples that go further down than up, the sorcerers are the aristocracy, and the whole country is treated by its neighbours as a source of very bad news drifting north. The tone is unmistakably the 1930s pulps' anxiety about the ancient world, and it has furnished every 'evil desert empire' since.

name: Svalbard
blurb: The kingdom of the armoured bears, who forge their own armour from sky-iron and regard it as their soul. There is a palace of ice, a deposed king, and a duel.
about: Pullman's panserbjørne are the best-realised non-humans in modern fantasy precisely because they are not people in fur: they cannot be tricked, except by appealing to the one thing they lack and want. Iorek Byrnison's armour is not clothing, it is the equivalent of a dæmon. The real Svalbard is a Norwegian archipelago you can fly to, with about 2,500 residents and considerably more polar bears than the tourist board mentions.

name: Talokan
blurb: A luminous city on the sea floor, older than anything above it, built by people who took a herb instead of smallpox and have spent five hundred years down there thinking about the surface.
about: Wakanda Forever's strongest idea is a second hidden civilisation with the same isolationist logic and a much worse memory of colonists: Namor's people fled a plague in the Yucatán and were changed by a plant into something that breathes water. The city is lit by an artificial sun, and the grievance behind it is entirely earned.

name: Talos IV
blurb: A blue-skied world of singing plants above and a city of enormous-brained illusionists below, who will show you anything you want and are the only planet under a Federation death penalty.

name: Taniquetil
blurb: The highest mountain in the world with the halls of Manwë on top of it — above the air, above the cloud, above the weather. The view is literally everything there is. It is also thirty below, and you were not invited.
about: From Ilmarin at the summit, Manwë and Varda can see the whole of Arda, and it was here that Varda made the stars. One mortal has ever reached those halls: Eärendil, arriving with a Silmaril bound to his brow to beg the Valar to intervene in the war. They did, and it ended the First Age and drowned a subcontinent doing it.

name: Tar Valon
blurb: A city of ogier-built towers on a river island, home to the White Tower and the only women in the world permitted to channel. Nobody enters a treaty with Tar Valon lightly.
about: The Aes Sedai are bound by three oaths — no lying, no making weapons, no using the One Power to kill except in defence — which makes them the most feared and least trusted people alive, because everyone knows exactly how much room those oaths leave. The Tower is split into seven Ajahs of different colours and purposes, and its politics are the slow, poisonous kind. The buildings were made by Ogier stonemasons and look grown rather than built.
photoTopics: Ile de la Cite Paris aerial

name: Tatooine
blurb: Twin suns, moisture farms and a spaceport bar with a strict no-droids policy. Nothing happens here, which is precisely why so much of it does.
photoTopics: Chott el Djerid Tunisia salt flat

name: Tauron
blurb: Dust, tobacco, bull statues and a civil war every other generation. The colony that exports soldiers, criminals and the best food in the Twelve, and does not discuss its feelings.
about: Adama is Tauron, which is why the story keeps coming back to it: a colony of farmers who fought a revolution, bury their dead in the ground rather than the sky, and are treated as gangsters everywhere richer. Caprica spends a season on the Ha'la'tha and on exactly what it costs a Tauron family to be respectable somewhere else.

name: Telos
blurb: An ice world whose original inhabitants were displaced by the Cybermen, who built vast refrigerated tombs beneath the surface and lay down in them to wait for somebody curious.

name: Terra Alpha
blurb: A human colony where unhappiness is a capital offence, enforced by women in pink and a robot made of confectionery. Everyone smiles. The disappearances are not discussed.

name: The Algae Planet
blurb: A barren world of algae fields and one four-thousand-year-old temple, orbiting a star that is going to explode on a schedule nobody controls. Bring a hazard suit and an open mind.
about: The fleet stops here because the algae is food, and finds the Temple of Five, built by the Thirteenth Tribe on their way to Earth. What follows is the series' best mysticism — an eclipse, a chamber of five faces, and Baltar being informed he is an instrument of God, shortly before a supernova is used as a weapon.

name: The Amity Fields
blurb: Orchards, greenhouses and communal singing on the far side of the fence, where everybody is relentlessly kind to one another and there is something baked into the bread.
about: Amity grow the food for the entire city and settle every dispute by consensus, which sounds idyllic until you find out what is in the loaves. The peace serum is Roth's sharpest idea: a faction that maintains its harmony chemically and genuinely cannot understand why an outsider would object to that.

name: The Argonath & Rauros
blurb: Two colossal stone kings guarding a river gorge, a long lake, and a waterfall that ends the boat journey for everybody. Best seen at dawn from something small, which is exactly how it is meant to be seen.
about: The Argonath are Isildur and Anárion, left hands raised in warning, carved when Gondor's northern border still meant something. Above the falls the Fellowship breaks: Frodo climbs Amon Hen, sits in the Seat of Seeing, and decides to go on alone. Rauros itself is a drop nobody portages in a hurry, and Boromir goes over it in a boat.

name: The Barrens
blurb: A vast yellow savanna of thorns, zhevras and one very long road, which takes an extremely long time to cross and is famous chiefly for the conversations people had while crossing it.
about: Barrens Chat is a genuine piece of internet folklore: a zone-wide chat channel in which a million players spent 2005 asking each other where Mankrik's wife was. The zone itself is deliberately empty and slow, and the Crossroads is a small outpost that becomes the emotional centre of anyone's first Horde character. Nostalgia for it is entirely disproportionate to its content, which is the point.

name: The Barrow-downs
blurb: Green hills, standing stones, a fog that arrives on schedule, and a great deal of gold in the ground with something cold sitting on it. Do not lie down against a stone.
about: The mounds are graves of the Dúnedain of Cardolan, and the wights in them were sent by Angmar to spoil the dead. The hobbits are robbed, buried and rescued here — and leave with daggers out of the hoard, one of which turns out to be the only blade in the West that can hurt the Witch-king. The whole detour looks like a digression and quietly wins the war.

name: The Blue Mountains
blurb: The dwarf-halls of the west: working mines, honest smiths, and the address Thorin Oakenshield used for a century and a half while he waited to get his mountain back. Cheaper than Erebor and half as smug.
about: Nogrod and Belegost stood in this range in the First Age — the dwarves who carved Menegroth and set the Silmaril in the Nauglamír — and both were ruined when the sea broke Beleriand. The Longbeards resettled the mountains in exile after Smaug took Erebor, and it is from a house here that Thorin sets out for Bag End and the worst-planned expedition in fiction.

name: The Bureau at O'Hare
blurb: A restored airport out past the ruins, where a government department has been watching the city through cameras for two hundred years and filing the results as a repair programme.
about: Allegiant's reveal is that the whole city is a laboratory: the Bureau of Genetic Welfare seeded the factions to breed damage out of the population, and has been observing the outcome, deaths included, without intervening once. The Fringe outside their perimeter is where everyone the experiment discarded actually lives.

name: The Capitol
blurb: A mountain-ringed city of astonishing wealth, cosmetic surgery and televised child murder, whose residents are genuinely puzzled that anyone resents them.
about: Collins built the Capitol out of imperial Rome — the names, the bread and circuses, the tribute system — and dressed it in reality-television gloss. The cruelty is not sadism so much as insulation: its citizens experience the Games as a sporting season and the districts as a supply chain. The food, the fashion and the parties are described in loving, nauseated detail, which is the book's real argument.

name: The Centre of the Earth
blurb: Down a dormant Icelandic volcano to a subterranean ocean lit by electrical discharge, with forests of giant mushrooms and things that should be extinct fighting in the shallows.
photoTopics: Journey to the Centre of the Earth engraving

name: The Citadel
blurb: A vast station of five arms and a central ring, capital of galactic civilisation, built by someone nobody has met. The wards go on for kilometres and the bureaucracy is worse.

name: The Cylon Colony
blurb: A vast accreted structure orbiting the event horizon of a naked singularity, grown rather than built, held together by a civil war it is losing. The last address anyone in this story visits.
about: The Colony is where the Cylons resurrect, where Hera is taken, and where the show finishes its shooting: Galactica jumps in alongside, rams it, and the two structures fall into the singularity together. It is one of the few sets in television science fiction that looks genuinely non-human — nothing is square and nothing was designed.

name: The Dawn of Man
blurb: A dry plain with one waterhole worth fighting over, a leopard in the rocks at night, and a black slab that appeared overnight and taught somebody to use a thigh bone as a hammer.
about: Twenty minutes without dialogue, and the whole argument of the film: the first tool is a weapon, the first act after learning to use it is a murder, and the bone thrown into the air becomes a spacecraft. Kubrick shot it on front-projected stills of Namibia and it still looks like nowhere on the current Earth.

name: The Dead Marshes
blurb: A flooded battlefield where the faces of the fallen show under the water. Uniquely atmospheric. Do not follow the lights.

name: The Death Star
blurb: A moon-sized battle station with a superlaser and, famously, a two-metre thermal exhaust port. Immaculate corridors, appalling health and safety, no handrails anywhere.

name: The Door of Night
blurb: A gate in the wall at the edge of everything, guarded permanently against one specific returning visitor, with the ship of Eärendil passing overhead on its way up. The last thing before there is nothing.
about: Beyond the Outer Sea stand the Walls of the World, and in them the Door of Night, through which Morgoth was thrust and through which the prophecy says he returns for the Dagor Dagorath. Eärendil sails above it with a Silmaril bound to his brow — the Evening Star, the one light left in Middle-earth that comes from the Trees, and the one Sam and Frodo look up at in Mordor and take heart from.

name: The Emerald City
blurb: A green city at the end of a yellow brick road, ruled by a wizard who turns out to be a balloonist from Omaha. Everyone is very kind and the spectacles are compulsory.
photoTopics: Denslow Wizard of Oz Emerald City

name: The Éothéod
blurb: Where the Rohirrim were before they were the Rohirrim: horse country in the cold north between the mountains and Mirkwood, a hall at Framsburg, and a family grudge involving a dragon.
about: The Éothéod moved north to the sources of Anduin around 1977 of the Third Age. Fram of that house killed the dragon Scatha and made a necklace of its teeth, which started a feud with the dwarves that outlived everyone involved. In 2510 Eorl the Young rode two thousand miles south to answer Gondor's call at the Field of Celebrant; Gondor gave him Calenardhon, and that is where Rohan comes from.

name: The Eyrie
blurb: A castle on a mountain spire reachable only by a mule track and three waystations. Impregnable, spectacular, and the sky cells have no fourth wall.

name: The Falas
blurb: Círdan's shipwright havens on the west coast: two walled harbours, the first great ships in the world, and the only elf-lord in the legendarium with a beard and no interest whatever in a crown.
about: Círdan has been building boats since before the sun rose and is still at it three ages later at the Grey Havens, which makes him the longest continuously running business in fiction. Morgoth broke the Falas in 473 and the survivors moved to the Isle of Balar — but every voyage west afterwards, Eärendil's included, goes in a hull his people built.
photoTopics: Sailing ship at anchor in bay

name: The Far Shore
blurb: White shores, and beyond them a far green country under a swift sunrise. The grey rain-curtain rolls back and the smell of the grass reaches you before the ship touches. Passage is one way.
about: The passage everyone quotes, and Tolkien gives it to Frodo twice — once as a dream in Bombadil's house near the start, and once for real at the end. He deliberately never describes what is inland: the destination is weather, light and the smell of cut grass, because anything more specific would have been an explanation, and this is the one place he refused to explain.
photoTopics: White sand beach clear sea dawn

name: The Forbidden Forest
blurb: Out of bounds to all pupils, which is why so much of every book happens there. Centaurs who read the stars and will not explain, acromantulas who will, and unicorns.
about: The forest is where the school's rules stop, and the series uses it as its consistent boundary between childhood and everything else — the first book's climax, the fifth book's escape, the seventh book's walk to the clearing. The centaurs refuse to intervene in human affairs on principle and resent being asked. Hagrid keeps things in there that he should not.

name: The Forest Moon of Endor
blurb: Thousand-foot redwoods, speeder bikes and a village of small hostile bears who will either eat you or crown you. Beautiful, and much more dangerous than it looks.

name: The Gardens of Lórien
blurb: Fountains, dim islands, drifting mist and the deepest sleep available anywhere in creation, kept by the Vala of dreams and his wife, who cures weariness. Purely a rest cure, and the best one there is.
about: Irmo's gardens are where the Valar themselves go to be soothed, and where Melian danced before she went to Middle-earth and married a king. Estë sleeps by day on the island in the lake of Lórellin and heals hurts of the spirit rather than the body. The elves borrowed the name for the Golden Wood, which is why time behaves strangely in both places.

name: The Gerudo Desert
blurb: Burning sand by day, freezing by night, and a walled town of warriors who bar men at the gate. The nearest thing Hyrule has to a city with an actual culture.
about: The Gerudo are a nation of women who produce one male child a century, and that child has an unfortunate track record. Gerudo Town enforces its no-men rule strictly enough that the games have made a running joke of the workarounds. The desert around it has sandstorms that disable your map, sinkholes with molduga in them, and a set of ruins that predate the kingdom.

name: The Gladden Fields
blurb: Miles of yellow iris in a slow green river, loud with birds, and somewhere in the mud the reason the whole story happens. Bring waders and a very long memory.
about: Isildur was ambushed here by orcs two years after the Ring was cut from Sauron's hand. He put it on, swam for it, and the Ring slipped off his finger and let him be shot in the water. It lay in the riverbed for two and a half thousand years until a Stoor named Déagol found it and his cousin Sméagol strangled him for it. Nothing at the site says any of this.

name: The Glade
blurb: Four stone walls a quarter of a mile high around a meadow, a wood, a farm and fifty boys who have been running the same experiment for three years without being told what it is.
about: The hook is the amnesia: nobody remembers anything but their own name, the walls close at sunset, and a box comes up out of the ground once a month with supplies and one more boy. What the Gladers have built out of that — rules, jobs, slang, a burial ground — is the best thing in the books.

name: The Glittering Caves
blurb: The most beautiful place in Middle-earth according to the only dwarf who ever saw it, and he was not sentimental about scenery. Bring a light, and someone to hold it.
about: Gimli finds Aglarond behind Helm's Deep during the battle and afterwards cannot stop talking about it — a rare passage where a character simply describes beauty for its own sake, and the argument that finally gets Legolas into a cave. He came back after the war with a company out of Erebor, founded a colony, and ended his life Lord of the Glittering Caves.

name: The Grey Havens
blurb: A quiet harbour at the end of everything, where white ships leave for the West. A one-way destination, and everyone knows it.

name: The Grizzly Hills
blurb: Autumn forest and log lodges on the edge of a frozen continent, with bears, lumber mills and the single most beloved piece of music anyone has written for a video game zone.
about: Northrend is otherwise an ice continent full of undead, and the Grizzly Hills is the warm exception — permanently in autumn, with woodsmoke and a fiddle-and-flute theme by Russell Brower that people put on to work to fifteen years later. The furbolg have a problem, the worgen have a worse one, and none of that is why anyone remembers the place.

name: The Halls of Aulë
blurb: The smith's mansions under the mountains of Aman: forges, workshops, drawing tables, and the chamber where the Dwarves were made too early and in secret by somebody who could not wait.
about: Aulë made the Seven Fathers of the Dwarves out of impatience, then offered to destroy them the moment he was caught — and Ilúvatar, who had been watching the whole time, adopted them instead and told him to put them back to sleep until the Elves had woken first. It is the warmest scene in The Silmarillion, and it is about a workaholic being forgiven.

name: The Halls of Mandos
region: The Shores of the Outer Sea
blurb: The houses of the dead: grey halls filling steadily with tapestries of everything that has ever happened, where the elves wait to be released and Men do not stay. Nobody arrives here on purpose.
about: Námo speaks twice in the whole legendarium and both times it is a doom nobody escapes. Lúthien is the one exception: she sang her way through these halls, moved him to pity for the first and only time, and got Beren back on condition of becoming mortal herself. The tapestries are woven by Vairë, and they are still being added to.

name: The Helcaraxë
blurb: The Grinding Ice: a moving strait of bergs and freezing fog between two continents, crossed on foot exactly once, out of pride. It killed a queen and much of a host, and the survivors arrived with the first moonrise.
about: Fëanor burned the ships and left his half-brother's people on the far shore, so Fingolfin's host walked across the ice rather than turn back — the most stubborn act in a legendarium built out of them. Elenwë died in the crossing. They came into Middle-earth as the Moon first rose and blew their trumpets at the gates of Angband, which is the best entrance anybody makes in any of the books.

name: The Hogwarts Express
blurb: A scarlet steam engine leaving King's Cross at eleven o'clock sharp and running eight hours north through increasingly dramatic scenery, with a trolley, a compartment of your own and nothing else to do.
about: The best-designed object in the series: a hard border between one life and the other, crossed twice a year, with the plot of each book set up in a compartment on the way. Rowling has admitted she is not sure why the platform is at King's Cross rather than Euston, beyond her parents having met on a train.

name: The Hub & the Fence
blurb: A walled Chicago two centuries after everything, with a marsh where the lake used to be, trains that never stop, and one skyscraper the whole city takes its name from. Nobody goes past the fence.
about: Roth's city is a closed experiment: five factions, one aptitude test, and a wall everybody has been told is keeping something out. The trains never stop because Dauntless jump on and off them at speed, which is the most efficient world-building in the book — you can identify somebody's faction by watching them board.

name: The Hundred Acre Wood
blurb: A small wood where the biggest problems are a stuck bear and a lost tail. Nothing bad has ever happened here and nothing bad ever will.
photoTopics: E H Shepard Winnie the Pooh illustration

name: The Ice Bay of Forochel
blurb: A frozen bay at the top of the world where the Lossoth live on the ice, eat what they catch, and tell visitors not to sail in winter. The last king of Arnor did not listen.
about: Arvedui, last king of the North, sheltered here after Angmar broke Fornost, and went down with his ship in the ice — the palantíri of Annúminas and Amon Sûl are still on the bottom of that bay. The Snowmen of Forochel stayed out of every war in the Third Age and are still there at the end of the book, which in this legendarium counts as winning.

name: The Imperial City
blurb: A ring of districts around a white tower on an island in a lake, at the exact centre of the continent. The Empire is administered from here, when there is one.
about: The White-Gold Tower was built by elves and taken by men, and the whole imperial project rests on it — which is why every crisis in the series involves something happening to it. The city's Arcane University, Arena and Market District are laid out as a wheel, an idea borrowed from Roman city planning and Dante alike. Cyrodiil is meant to be the boring province, and is: temperate, orderly, and full of paperwork.

name: The Iron Islands
blurb: Wet rock in a cold sea, populated by people who consider farming beneath them and raiding a career. They do not sow. They also do not have much.

name: The Island of Utopia
blurb: Fifty-four identical cities, six-hour working days, gold used for chamber pots, and no private property whatsoever. Immaculately reasonable and quietly unnerving.

name: The Ivory Tower
blurb: A white spiral at the centre of a land made entirely of human imagination, where the Childlike Empress is dying because too few people are still making things up.
about: Fantastica has no borders, because imagination has none, and it is being eaten by the Nothing — a hole that appears wherever people stop believing. The Empress cannot act; she can only wait for a human child to give her a new name. Ende's second half, which the 1984 film omits entirely, is about what happens to someone who can wish for anything: every wish costs a memory, and you can wish yourself into having nothing left to wish with.

name: The Kingdom of Lancre
blurb: A small mountain kingdom you could walk across in a day, mostly vertical, held together by three witches who would strongly prefer you did not need them.
about: Lancre sits on a magical fault line, which is why the local witches — Granny Weatherwax, Nanny Ogg and whoever is currently third — spend most of their time keeping things out rather than letting things in. Witchcraft here is not spells but headology: knowing exactly what people already believe and using it on them. Excellent cheese. Do not accept a drink from Nanny Ogg.

name: The Land of the Houyhnhnms
blurb: A country of rational, virtuous horses who keep degenerate humans as livestock. Deeply peaceful, deeply humbling, and you will not enjoy how you are classified.

name: The Lantern Waste
blurb: A snow-covered wood where a working iron lamp-post stands in the middle of nowhere, marking the place where a wardrobe lets out. Always winter here, until it isn't.
about: The lamp-post grew from a fragment of London street furniture dropped into new-made soil at the creation of the world, which is the sort of joke Lewis enjoyed. This is the first Narnia anyone sees, and for a hundred years it was held under the White Witch's permanent winter with no Christmas. The thaw, when it comes, is described more vividly than any battle in the series.

name: The Library
blurb: An entire planet built as a library, holding every book ever written, with a moon that stops the pages rotting. Silent for a hundred years, and the shadows on the floor are not all shadows.

name: The Lone Islands & the Eastern Sea
blurb: Sail east past the Lone Islands and the sea gets stranger — an island where dreams come true, one that turns things to gold, and finally water you can drink and light you can eat.
about: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader is the best of the seven, and it is the one with the least plot: a boat sails east and things get progressively more numinous until the water turns sweet and lilies grow on it. Eustace becomes a dragon through pure greed and is un-dragoned painfully by Aslan, which is the most honest thing Lewis wrote about being forgiven.

name: The Maze
blurb: Stone corridors a hundred feet high that rearrange themselves every night, mapped by teenagers at a dead run and patrolled after dark by machines with too many legs. There is no way out. That is not the same as no exit.
about: The maze is a test, not a prison: the people watching want to know which patterns of thought show up under lethal pressure, and the walls move in a sequence that spells out words for anyone stubborn enough to chart it for two years. The Grievers are the least interesting thing in it.

name: The Meneltarma
blurb: The Pillar of Heaven: a mountain in the middle of the island climbed three times a year in complete silence, with eagles overhead and no building of any kind on top.
about: Númenor had no temple and no priests — only a summit where the king spoke to Ilúvatar three times a year, and a rule that nobody says a word on the way up. Then the last kings stopped going and built a temple to Morgoth instead. When the island sank the peak may have been left as an island; mariners looked for it for centuries and never found it.

name: The Ministry of Magic
blurb: A vast underground bureaucracy reached by flushing yourself down a toilet, with an enchanted ceiling, a fountain of dubious taste, and a courtroom nobody wants to visit.
about: The Ministry is Rowling's best joke and her sharpest point: magic administered by civil servants, with a Department of Mysteries nobody understands and a press office that lies. The Atrium's fountain shows a wizard being adored by grateful magical creatures, which everyone walks past daily without noticing what it says.

name: The Misty Mountains
blurb: A thousand-mile spine of snow, storm and things living under it. The passes are worse than they look, and they look bad.
photoTopics: Southern Alps New Zealand snow peaks

name: The Mushroom Kingdom
blurb: Cheerful hills, floating brick blocks, warp pipes to everywhere and physics that reward jumping. The princess is in another castle, but the castle is very nice.
about: There is no consistent map, no real history and no explanation for the pipes, and none of that has ever mattered — the kingdom exists to be moved through, and its geography is designed around the arc of a jump. Miyamoto's rule was that the first eight seconds should teach you everything; those eight seconds are World 1-1, which is probably the most studied level design in the world.
photoTopics: Rolling green hills blue sky clouds

name: The Nameless Deeps
region: Beneath the Roots of the Mountains
blurb: Far below the deepest delving of the dwarves, where the world is gnawed by things that have no name and no maker. Gandalf went down there, came back, and would not say what he saw.
about: Far, far beneath the deepest delving of the Dwarves, the world is gnawed by nameless things. Even Sauron knows them not. They are older than he. Gandalf refuses to describe them — lest it darken the light of day — which is the most effective restraint in all of Tolkien: the only thing in the legendarium that frightens a Maia who has just fought a Balrog to a standstill.

name: The Nine Circles
blurb: A descending funnel of nine circles, each with a punishment precisely fitted to its sin, ending in a frozen lake rather than fire. Abandon all hope, etc.

name: The Nox Forest
blurb: An old forest whose people are so far ahead of you that they have no interest in weapons, no interest in your war, and a city they keep hidden in the air above the trees until they need it.
about: The Nox raise the dead, hide an entire floating city, and politely decline to help anybody's military — the first time Stargate suggests that being more advanced might mean caring less about the plot. The very young do not always do as they are told is the most graceful dressing-down in the franchise.

name: The Off-World Colonies
blurb: A new life awaits you in the off-world colonies! The chance to begin again in a golden land of opportunity and adventure. Terms and conditions have never once been shown on screen.
about: The blimp advertisement is the most famous thing in the film that is never depicted. Everyone with options has gone; replicants are built to do the work out there; and the entire plot is four of them coming back because it is so bad. The colonies are pure salesmanship, and the reason the city below is empty of anyone who could leave.

name: The Old Forest
blurb: A wood that moves its paths while you are walking them, a river that sings you to sleep, and a man in yellow boots older than all of it who sings back. Nothing here is on your side except him.
about: Tom Bombadil has no explanation and Tolkien refused to supply one: he is Eldest, the Ring does nothing to him, and he is completely uninterested in the war. His wood is the oldest thing left in Eriador and it holds a grudge against anyone carrying an axe, which given the history is not unreasonable. The barrow-blades the hobbits are armed with come out of his house.

name: The Pit
blurb: A cavern under the city with rooms cut into its walls, a chasm running through the middle of it with no railings anywhere, and an initiation process that publishes a failure rate.
about: Dauntless live underground and treat the entire faction as a dare: no handrails, a zip line off the tallest building left standing, and initiates cut for placing badly. The chasm is where the bravery cult stops being fun, and the book is perfectly clear that not all of those falls were accidents.

name: The Psi-Moon
blurb: A moon terraformed to mirror the mind of whoever lands on it. Land one self-loathing hologram and you get a swamp of low self-esteem, a gothic fortress of his hang-ups, and a hooded thing called the Unspeakable One.
about: Psi-moons were built so psychiatric patients could walk around inside their own heads. Rimmer's turns out to be a bog, with his self-respect held prisoner in a castle and his cowardice riding about as a knight. It is the most literal joke the show ever made and somehow its most sympathetic: the landscape is an honest diagnosis.

name: The Quantum Realm
blurb: Underneath the smallest thing there is: a place with no time, its own weather, its own cities and civilisations, and a woman who spent thirty years down there learning things nobody wanted to hear.
about: Ant-Man's subatomic layer began as a way to lose a character and turned into an entire cosmology — probability storms, freedom fighters, a conqueror in exile, and time behaving so badly that five hours down here is five years up there. It is also the sole mechanism by which the Infinity Saga is eventually undone.

name: The Quidditch World Cup
blurb: A hundred thousand witches and wizards camped on a moor around a stadium that was not there last week: a week of queues, souvenir hawkers, tents with four bedrooms inside, and one very good match.
about: The campsite is the best sustained comedy in the books — wizards failing to dress as Muggles, an Irish supporter with a shamrock-shaped tent, a Ministry official arguing about a chimney. Then it turns, and masked men walk through the tents at midnight holding a family in the air. It is the chapter where the series stops being about school.

name: The Reach
blurb: The richest and most fertile part of Westeros — orchards, vineyards, tourneys and courtly manners laid thickly over the usual amount of scheming.
about: The Reach is where Westeros keeps its idea of chivalry, which mostly means the knights there are better dressed rather than better behaved. Its lords have spent three hundred years insisting on a claim to be Kings of the Reach that everyone politely ignores. The wine is genuinely the best in the Seven Kingdoms, and the Arbor's is the best of that.

name: The Ring of Doom
blurb: A circle of thrones on a hill outside the western gate of Valimar, unroofed, where the Powers of the world sit in council. Judgements pronounced here are not appealed, and have never once been overturned.
about: The Máhanaxar is where the Valar summon Fëanor to answer for himself, where Melkor is released on parole against everybody's better judgement, and where Mandos pronounces the Doom of the Noldor over a shore full of people who then sail anyway. Nearly everything that goes wrong in the First Age is decided, or wrongly forgiven, inside this circle.

name: The Rings of Akhaten
blurb: Seven worlds orbiting one star, where a pyramid holds something old and hungry and the entrance fee is a song. Payment everywhere is sentimental: rings, keepsakes, things you cannot bear to lose.

name: The Ringworld
blurb: A band of engineered land circling a star, with three million times Earth's surface area and a civilisation that has forgotten how any of it works.

name: The Riverlands
blurb: Where every road in Westeros crosses and every war is fought. Green, wet, and comprehensively burned down at least once a generation.
about: Riverrun sits in the fork of two rivers and can flood its own moat, which is the single best piece of castle design in the books. The Riverlands' misfortune is geography: they are in the middle, so everyone marches through, and the smallfolk pay for all of it. The Red Wedding happens here, at a bridge nobody could avoid using.

name: The Safe Haven
blurb: A green valley behind a mountain range on an island the flares never reached, handed over with tools, seeds and instructions. The first place in three books with no cameras in it.
about: The series ends with a door in a wall and a valley on the other side: forest, a river, a beach and no observers. After three books of surveillance the whole point of the ending is the absence of an audience — the survivors finally get to be unremarkable, which is the only reward left to give them.

name: The San Diego Scrap Yard
blurb: A hundred square miles of ships being taken apart by children with hammers, run as a going concern by a man who describes it as a business opportunity. The rain is worse here than in the city.
about: In 2049 San Diego is where things are sent to be dismantled, and where orphans are put to work stripping circuits out of hulls. It is the one look the films give you at the labour holding this world up: no neon, no replicants, just wet metal and small hands. Everything in this future is old and being broken down for parts, including the people.

name: The Scorch
blurb: What is left of the middle of a continent after the solar flares: sand over a city, lightning storms that bring no rain, and the infected living in whatever buildings are still standing.
about: The Scorch is the series' best landscape — a dead metropolis half buried, crossed on foot, under electrical storms. The virus takes the mind well before the body, and the middle stage is where the horror actually lives: people who know exactly what is happening to them and can still hold a conversation about it.

name: The Sea of Rhûn
blurb: A freshwater sea in the middle of an ocean of grass, with wain-riders on the shore, horse herds, chariots, and the road that brings Dorwinion wine west. Everything Gondor calls the East begins here.
about: The Easterlings have come west three times in recorded history; the Wainriders nearly finished Gondor in 1944 and killed a king doing it. Dorwinion, on the south-western shore, grows the wine that eventually gets thirteen dwarves out of Thranduil's cells. Beyond the sea the maps stop, and it is out there that two of the five wizards went and never came back.

name: The Shattered Plains
blurb: A thousand square miles of plateaus separated by chasms, scoured every few days by storms that would strip the skin off you. The war fought across it has lasted six years and achieved nothing.
about: Roshar's ecology is built around the highstorms: the plants retract into shells, the animals are crustaceans, and there is no grass that does not hide. The plateaus are the shattered remains of something, and the chasms between them are full of bones, gemhearts and one very large predator. Sanderson wrote the bridge crews — men used as expendable equipment — as the emotional engine of the first book.

name: The Shire
blurb: Rolling green farmland, six meals a day and a deep suspicion of anything that happens. The single most restful destination in fiction, provided nobody knocks on your door about a quest.
photoTopics: Waikato rolling green farmland New Zealand

name: The Smoking Sea & Valyria
blurb: The greatest empire that ever lived, destroyed in a single day and still burning four hundred years later. Nobody who sails in comes back healthy.

name: The Star Gate
blurb: Ten minutes of coloured light at impossible speed, and then a neoclassical hotel suite with a lit floor, a made bed and a meal laid out, where you will age through the rest of your life in an afternoon.
about: Nobody explains it, and the novel published alongside the film explains it far too well. The room is the part that lasts: whoever built it assembled a human habitat from broadcast television, got the details subtly wrong, and left a man to grow old in it politely. Then the glass breaks, and something is watching from the foot of the bed.

name: The Tech-Com Tunnels
blurb: Storm drains and service tunnels holding a few hundred people, a dog on every entrance to sniff out infiltrators, and one working piece of equipment that can send a person back forty-five years.
about: The Resistance runs on dogs, hand-drawn maps and salvage. Connor's people take Skynet's defence grid apart from underneath, which is why the machine's last move is to attack his mother instead — and why the time-displacement equipment gets used exactly twice before it is destroyed. Everything the story does happens because of one bunker.

name: The Time Variance Authority
blurb: An office outside time with beige corridors, a ticketing system, a cartoon clock who cheerfully explains your execution, and an entire filing department for realities that were pruned for going off script.
about: Bureaucratic dread played for laughs: mid-century office furniture, laminated procedure, and a workforce of abducted variants who have been told they were created for the job. For All Time. Always. is a motivational slogan on the wall of an organisation that deletes universes for administrative tidiness.

name: The Timeless Halls
blurb: Where the Ainur were made and the Music was sung: no world yet, no time yet, nothing but the halls of Ilúvatar and a theme being taken up in parts. Everything since has been a performance of what was sung here.
about: The Ainulindalë is the first thing in The Silmarillion and the strangest. Ilúvatar propounds a theme, the Ainur sing it, Melkor sings against it, and the discord is woven back in so that the worst of history turns out to have been part of the composition all along. Then Ilúvatar says Eä — let it Be — and the singers who go down into the world become the Valar. They do not come back.

name: The Two Rivers
blurb: Sheep, tabac and the best wool in the world, in a corner of the map so quiet that its people have forgotten they were once the last soldiers of a fallen nation.
about: Jordan's deliberate echo of the Shire: an ordinary farming district whose ordinariness is the whole point, and out of which walk three of the most consequential people in the world. The Women's Circle and the Village Council disagree about everything and run the place perfectly well. It is also, quietly, the remnant of Manetheren, a kingdom that died refusing to surrender — which becomes relevant.

name: The Tyrell Corporation
blurb: Seven hundred storeys of ziggurat standing above the smog with its own private sunset, an artificial owl in the lobby, and a proprietor who will explain very kindly why your lifespan cannot be extended.
about: The pyramid is the only place in the film with daylight, because Tyrell has simply built above the weather. Everything about it is a temple — the scale, the candles, the man at the top who made you and cannot fix you. The light that burns twice as bright burns half as long is the mission statement of a company whose product is a four-year person.

name: The Visitor Centre
blurb: A half-finished rotunda with two skeletons in the atrium, a banner reading When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth, and a kitchen everybody remembers for the wrong reasons. Abandoned mid-construction, twice.
about: The centre is the film's whole thesis in one building: a museum about extinction, unfinished, in a park that has already failed, with the mounted fossils of the animals currently outside in the rain. Spielberg drops the banner across the frame at the end because he could not resist, and it is still the best closing shot in the franchise.

name: The Void
blurb: The Everlasting Dark outside the world, containing nothing whatsoever except Morgoth, who was thrown into it through a door that is guarded. No floor, no end, no other guests.
about: Melkor went into the Void looking for the Flame Imperishable and did not find it, because it is with Ilúvatar — the first thing that goes wrong in creation, and everything else follows from it. After the War of Wrath the Valar thrust him out through the Door of Night, and the prophecy says he comes back through it for the last battle. Until then this is the emptiest destination available anywhere.

name: The Vorlon Homeworld
blurb: Nobody goes to the Vorlon homeworld. Nobody sees a Vorlon. Nobody asks a Vorlon a straight question and gets a straight answer, and understanding is, apparently, a three-edged sword.
about: The Vorlons appear as angels to every younger race because they engineered themselves into everyone's mythology, and the series spends four years letting you assume they are the good side before showing what that arrangement costs. The homeworld is glimpsed once, briefly, and it does not look like anywhere.

name: The Wall
blurb: Seven hundred feet of ice running three hundred miles, manned by an order of convicts and younger sons. The view from the top is unmatched and the posting is for life.

name: The Wallace Corporation
blurb: Golden rooms lined with rippling water-light, absolute silence, and a blind proprietor who has solved the food supply and regards people as a manufacturing problem. Tyrell was warmer.
about: Wallace ended the famine with synthetic farming and then bought what was left of Tyrell, and 2049 gives him the emptiest and most beautiful interiors in either film — all gold, all reflected off water, nobody else in the room. His archive holds a record of every replicant ever made, and the plot turns on one entry in it: who is allowed to have had a childhood.

name: The Wine-Dark Sea
blurb: Island-hop between a cyclops, a witch who turns men into pigs, sirens, and a whirlpool. Ten years is the standard itinerary. Hospitality is sacred, and so is revenge.

name: The Withered Heath
blurb: A dry valley in the Grey Mountains where the great worms breed. This is where dragons come from, and every dwarf-hall in the north was emptied by something that started here.
about: Tolkien mentions the Withered Heath twice and never takes you there, which is why it is the most frightening address in the north. Scatha came out of these mountains, and so did the cold-drake that killed Dáin I and drove the Longbeards south to Erebor — the migration that puts a dwarf-kingdom under a lonely mountain and, eventually, a dragon on top of it. The Hobbit starts here.

name: The Woodland Realm
blurb: Thranduil's halls under a hill behind a river gate: torchlight, singing, seriously good wine and a king with a grievance. Also a very well-appointed set of cells, as thirteen dwarves found out.
about: The Silvan elves are the least lofty in the books and by some distance the most fun — feasts in the open woods, Dorwinion wine strong enough to put a butler to sleep, a king openly and pettily interested in gems. Thranduil is also the only leader in The Hobbit who marches on Erebor for a share of the treasure and then drops the claim the moment it stops being reasonable.

name: Tirion upon Túna
blurb: A white city on a green hill in a mountain pass, with a silver lamp on a tower that can be seen from the sea. Built by the Noldor, half-emptied by them in a single night, and still lit.
about: Tirion is where Fëanor made the Silmarils and gave the speech that took a third of his people out of Aman for good. Finarfin turned back at the shore and rules what is left. Everything the Noldor do in Middle-earth over the next six centuries is an attempt to justify having walked out of this city, and most of them never see it again.

name: Titan
blurb: A dead world with its own moons in pieces overhead and gravity that no longer agrees with itself, ruined by precisely the overpopulation its most famous son later proposed to fix everywhere else.
about: Titan is the argument the whole Infinity Saga is built on. Thanos says he warned them, that his solution was random and dispassionate and would have saved the place, and the film lets him say it standing in the rubble of the evidence. The set is pure Dali: broken rings, floating masonry, a sun through dust.

name: Tol Eressëa
blurb: The Lonely Isle, moored within sight of Aman, with the haven of Avallónë facing east and every ship that ever left Middle-earth for good tied up in it. This is where the elves you have been reading about went.
about: Tol Eressëa was towed across the sea twice as a ferry and then anchored in the bay for good. Everyone who sails from the Grey Havens lands at Avallónë — Frodo and Bilbo, Sam long afterwards, and Gimli, the only dwarf ever to go. It is the nearest thing the legendarium has to a retirement, and Tolkien only ever lets you see it from the far side of the water.

name: Tollana
blurb: An immaculate city belonging to people who will not share their technology with you, at all, ever, and who turn out to have been entirely right about why. Ion cannons on the ridge; superb public transport.
about: The Tollan refuse to give humans anything, because the last time they helped a neighbouring civilisation that civilisation destroyed itself within a generation. They are proved right, and then killed anyway when the Goa'uld arrive with ships their cannons cannot touch. Stargate's grimmest hour is about a smug people being correct and losing regardless.

name: Trantor
blurb: Forty billion people under a continuous metal dome covering the whole planet, and the Imperial Library where a mathematician worked out exactly how it all ends.

name: Trenzalore
blurb: A snowbound town called Christmas where nobody can tell a lie, kept in permanent siege by every enemy the Doctor ever made, and rather lovely between attacks.

name: Trill
blurb: A temperate world of lakes and universities, and beneath it the Caves of Mak'ala, where the symbionts live in pools and a small committee decides who gets to carry several lifetimes of memory.

name: Tuzanor
blurb: The City of Sorrows on Minbar: gardens, thin cold air, a bell that rings for the dead of a war nobody won, and an academy that trains people to go out and not come back.
about: Tuzanor is where the Anla'shok are made — Delenn's Rangers, drawn from Minbari and humans both, trained to watch and to report and, when it comes to it, to die quietly a long way from home. The show puts its most reflective scenes here: a city named for grief that keeps a very good garden.

name: Überwald
blurb: Dark forests, castles on crags and a vampire aristocracy going through a difficult modernisation. The werewolves are the reasonable ones. Mind the dwarf mines.
about: Every Central European gothic cliché, gathered in one place and then quietly interrogated. The vampires have formed a temperance league and wear black ribbons; the werewolves have a monarchy; the dwarfs are having an argument about whether female dwarfs are allowed to admit they exist. Pratchett's point is always that the monsters are managing, and the trouble comes from anyone insisting they go back to being monsters.

name: Umbar
blurb: The greatest natural harbour in the world, full of black ships crewed by people whose great-grandparents were Gondorians and who would burn Gondor to the waterline given a fair wind.
about: Umbar is where the Black Númenóreans went — the faction that stayed loyal to Sauron — so the war with Gondor is a family quarrel three thousand years old. Ar-Pharazôn landed here to take Sauron prisoner, which worked for about fifty years and then destroyed Númenor. The great pillar raised to commemorate it stood over the haven until the corsairs pulled it down.

name: Underland
blurb: A sunless kingdom of gnomes and lamplight, a silver chair, and a queen who will patiently explain that there is no sun, no Narnia and no Aslan, until you believe her.
about: The Silver Chair contains the single best scene in the series: the witch throwing enchanted powder on the fire and arguing, reasonably and gently, that the overworld is something the characters invented. Puddleglum puts his foot in the fire to clear his head and says he will go on living like a Narnian even if there isn't one. It is a better argument than most philosophy manages.

name: Unseen University
blurb: The Discworld's premier college of magic, whose faculty long ago worked out that the surest way to avoid magical catastrophe is an enormous lunch. The Library is not shelved in three dimensions.
about: Wizards here are not adventurers; they are academics with very large hats and a serious interest in the dinner rota. The Librarian was turned into an orangutan and declined to be turned back, since it improved his reach. L-space — the principle that all libraries are connected because sufficient books warp reality — is the university's one genuinely dangerous idea, and it is guarded by an ape with a banana.

name: Urithiru
blurb: A tower city of a hundred levels carved into a mountain above the storms, with a garden at the top that grows without soil and a lift system nobody has repaired in millennia.
about: Abandoned for four thousand years and rediscovered by people with no manual. Urithiru sits above the highstorms — the only place on Roshar that does — and is connected to every other Radiant city by a network of portals in its basement. Sanderson's worldbuilding runs on rules: the tower has a mind, the mind has been asleep, and waking it turns out to have consequences that are entirely foreshadowed.

name: Valimar
blurb: The city of the Valar: bells, golden streets, and the powers of the world keeping house and holding council. Nobody who has been there has ever managed to describe it without going quiet.
about: Valimar stands on the plain beyond the Pelóri, with the Two Trees outside its western gate and the halls of Manwë above it on Taniquetil. Galadriel's lament in Lothlórien is homesickness for this specific city — who now shall refill the cup for me? — and the whole grief of the Noldor is that they left it and cannot get back. The bells of Valimar are the last thing in her song.

name: Villengard
blurb: Once the galaxy's largest weapons factory, now a banana grove, following an incident the Doctor declines to elaborate on. Bananas are good; you should always bring a banana to a party.

name: Volantis
blurb: The oldest daughter of Valyria, split by the Rhoyne and the Long Bridge, hot enough that the elephants move slowly. Five slaves to every free man, and a red temple that never sleeps.

name: Vormir
blurb: A dead red world with a cliff at the top of a mountain, permanent overcast, and a guide who knows your name, your history and exactly what the Soul Stone is going to cost you.
about: Vormir's keeper is the Red Skull, exiled here by the Tesseract and made caretaker of a stone he can never hold — the tidiest piece of housekeeping in the whole franchise. The price is fixed and cannot be negotiated: a soul for a soul, someone you love, over the edge. Two films put their emotional weight on that cliff.

name: Vortis
blurb: An airless world of acid pools and volcanic craters, webbed over by something malevolent, and home to the Menoptra — a civilisation of enormous, courteous butterflies.

name: Vulcan
blurb: A hot, thin-aired desert world of monasteries and forge-red rock, populated by people who suppressed their emotions and have been quietly smug about it for two thousand years.

name: Vvardenfell
blurb: An ash-covered volcanic island of giant mushroom towers, insect transport and three living gods with a public relations problem. Nothing here looks like anywhere else.
about: The most deliberately alien setting in mainstream fantasy: the houses are grown from fungus or carved from beetle shells, the taxi service is a giant flea, and the state religion is run by three people who made themselves divine and are now watching it wear off. The ash storms are genuinely dangerous and the local disease will turn you into something. Bethesda has never made anything this strange again.

name: Wakanda
blurb: A nation that hid itself for centuries behind a projection of farmland while building the most advanced city on Earth on top of the world's only vibranium deposit.
about: Created by Lee and Kirby in 1966 as a direct rebuttal to how Africa was drawn in comics, and rebuilt by Ta-Nehisi Coates and the 2018 film into something with a working political argument: what a country owes the world when it has never been colonised and could help. The tribal council, the Dora Milaje and the herb-granted throne are all bound up in the succession, which is settled by ritual combat at a waterfall.

name: Waterdeep
blurb: The City of Splendours: a huge, wealthy port run by masked Lords nobody can identify, sitting on top of the largest dungeon in the world.
about: Waterdeep is where every Forgotten Realms campaign starts, because it has a guild for everything, a tavern for every kind of trouble and Undermountain directly beneath it — a dungeon of more than twenty levels built by a mad wizard who is still down there and still redecorating. The Lords wear enchanted masks in public so that assassinating them achieves nothing. Baldur's Gate is a few weeks' ride south and considerably less pleasant.

name: Waxworld
blurb: An abandoned waxwork theme park on a colony world, left running long enough for the droids to declare war: Hero World against Villain World, Elvis and Gandhi against Caligula and the Third Reich, in earnest.
about: The concept is the whole episode — wax droids carrying the memories of the people they depict, no supervision, and enough centuries to develop politics. Rimmer takes command of the good side because he has always wanted to be a general and marches them into a massacre, and Kryten wins the war by rewiring a pacifist.

name: Weathertop
blurb: A bare hill with a broken ring of stone on top and a clear view of the road in both directions — which is exactly why everyone camps there, and exactly why they should not.
about: Amon Sûl held the chief palantír of the North and was burned in the wars with Angmar. What is left is a crown of tumbled masonry and a hollow where Frodo is stabbed with a Morgul blade and starts dying slowly for the next fortnight. The point of the hill was always that you can see anyone coming; nobody ever mentions that they can see you.

name: Whitefall
blurb: A fourth moon of Athens with maybe two thousand settlers, one crime boss called Patience, and a great deal of open grass. She has shot a visitor before. She will probably do it again.

name: WICKED Headquarters
blurb: A clean white research facility where a department of adults keeps orphaned children in a maze, films them dying, and files the resulting paperwork as progress. The signage says WICKED is good.
about: The acronym is the tell. The organisation believes the killzone patterns harvested from traumatised children will produce a vaccine for a virus that has already taken civilisation, and the books never quite let them be simply wrong — the argument that some price is worth paying is given to people you are meant to find reasonable.

name: Winterfell
blurb: A granite castle built over hot springs, so the walls stay warm while everything outside freezes. Excellent hosts, if you survive the feast.

name: Wonderland
blurb: A croquet ground with flamingos, a permanent tea party, and a queen with strong views on beheading. Nothing here follows from anything else and everyone finds you rude.

name: Wrigley's Pleasure Planet
blurb: Mentioned once, in passing, as the place crews go on leave and do not describe afterwards. The entire economy is diversion, and the brochures are considerably more discreet than the reviews.

name: Xandar
blurb: The Nova Corps capital: clean plazas, competent police who fly in formation, and the best civic architecture in the galaxy. Later destroyed off-screen, which nobody has forgiven.
about: Xandar is the one properly functional civilisation in the cosmic half of this universe — the Corps hold the line, the citizens are decent, and the film presents the place as worth defending, which is why the finale works. That it is then wiped out between films, in a line of dialogue, is the most casual destruction in the franchise.

name: Xelaya
blurb: A beautiful, cultured world with gravity so high its people are superhumanly strong anywhere else and increasingly fragile at home. Excellent architecture, exceptional universities, take the lift.

name: Yavin 4
blurb: A jungle moon of a gas giant, with Massassi temples rising above the canopy. Humid, loud with insects, and historically good for hiding a fleet.

name: Yonada
blurb: A generation ship disguised inside an asteroid, whose people believe their sky is the sky and that the Oracle punishing blasphemers is a god rather than a rather stern computer.

name: Z'ha'dum
blurb: A dead world with a very old city buried underneath it, home to something that has been arranging galactic wars for its own reasons for a million years. People who go there do not come back.
